{{Short description|Formulation of classical mechanics}}
{{Use American English|date = February 2019}}
[[File:Langrange portrait.jpg|thumb|150px|[[Joseph-Louis Lagrange]] (1736–1813)]]
{{Classical mechanics|cTopic=Formulations}}

In [[physics]], '''Lagrangian mechanics''' is an alternate formulation of [[classical mechanics]] founded on the [[D'Alembert's principle|d'Alembert principle]] of virtual work. It was introduced by the Italian-French mathematician and astronomer [[Joseph-Louis Lagrange]] in his presentation to the Turin Academy of Science in 1760<ref>Fraser, Craig. "J. L. Lagrange's Early Contributions to the Principles and Methods of Mechanics". Archive for History of Exact Sciences, vol. 28, no. 3, 1983, pp. 197–241. JSTOR, http://www.jstor.org/stable/41133689. Accessed 3 Nov. 2023.</ref> culminating in his 1788 grand opus, ''[[Mécanique analytique]]''.<ref>{{harvnb|Hand|Finch|1998|page=23}}</ref> Lagrange's approach greatly simplifies the analysis of many problems in mechanics, and it had crucial influence on other branches of physics, including relativity and quantum field theory.

Lagrangian mechanics describes a mechanical system as a pair {{nowrap|(''M'', ''L'')}} consisting of a [[configuration space (physics)|configuration space]] ''M'' and a smooth function <math display="inline">L</math> within that space called a ''Lagrangian''. For many systems, {{nowrap|1=''L'' = ''T'' − ''V''}}, where ''T'' and ''V'' are the [[Kinetic energy|kinetic]] and [[Potential energy|potential]] energy of the system, respectively.<ref>{{harvnb|Hand|Finch|1998|pages=18–20}}</ref>

The stationary action principle requires that the [[Action (physics)#Action (functional)|action functional]] of the system derived from ''L'' must remain at a [[stationary point]] (specifically, a [[Maximum and minimum|maximum]], [[Maximum and minimum|minimum]], or [[Saddle point|saddle]] point) throughout the time evolution of the system. This constraint allows the calculation of the equations of motion of the system using Lagrange's equations.<ref>{{harvnb|Hand|Finch|1998|pages=46,51}}</ref>

== Introduction ==

[[File:Bead on wire constraint.svg|thumb|Bead constrained to move on a frictionless wire. The wire exerts a reaction force '''C''' on the bead to keep it on the wire. The non-constraint force '''N''' in this case is gravity. Notice the initial position of the bead on the wire can lead to different motions.]]
[[File:Pendulum constraint.svg|upright=0.7|thumb|Simple pendulum. Since the rod is rigid, the position of the bob is constrained according to the equation {{nowrap|1=''f''(''x'', ''y'') = 0}}, the constraint force C is the tension in the rod. Again the non-constraint force '''N''' in this case is gravity.]]

Newton's laws and the concept of forces are the usual starting point for teaching about mechanical systems.<ref name=Ball2019>{{Cite journal |last=Ball |first=Philip |date=2019-09-13 |title=Teaching Energy Before Forces |url=https://physics.aps.org/articles/v12/100 |access-date=2024-09-27 |journal=Physics |volume=12 |issue=2 |page=100 |language=en |doi=10.1103/PhysRevPhysEducRes.15.020126|bibcode=2019PRPER..15b0126L |hdl=1808/29610 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> This method works well for many problems, but for others the approach is prohibitively complicated.<ref name=TatumClassNotes>{{Cite web |last=Tatum |first=J. B. |title=Lagrangian mechanics |url=https://www.astro.uvic.ca/~tatum/classmechs/class13.pdf |access-date=2024-09-27 |website=www.astro.uvic.ca}}</ref> For example, calculation of the motion of a [[torus]] rolling on a horizontal surface with a pearl sliding inside, the time-varying constraint forces like the [[angular velocity]] of the torus and the motion of the pearl in relation to the torus made it difficult to determine the motion of the torus with Newton's equations.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last1=Parsons |first1=Paul |title=50 ideas you really need to know: science |last2=Dixon |first2=Gail |publisher=[[Quercus]] |year=2016 |isbn=978-1-78429-614-8 |location=London |pages=4–7 |language=en}}</ref> Lagrangian mechanics adopts energy rather than force as its basic ingredient,<ref name=Ball2019/> leading to more abstract equations capable of tackling more complex problems.<ref name=TatumClassNotes/>

Particularly, Lagrange's approach was to set up independent [[generalized coordinate]]s for the position and speed of every object, which allows the writing down of a general form of the Lagrangian (total kinetic energy minus potential energy of the system) and summing this over all possible paths of motion of the particles yielded a formula for the 'action', which he minimized to give a generalized set of equations. This summed quantity is minimized along the path that the particle actually takes. This choice eliminates the need for the constraint force to enter into the resultant generalized [[system of equations]]. There are fewer equations since one is not directly calculating the influence of the constraint on the particle at a given moment.<ref name=":0" />

For a wide variety of physical systems, if the size and shape of a massive object are negligible, it is a useful simplification to treat it as a [[point particle]]. For a system of ''N'' point particles with [[mass]]es ''m''<sub>1</sub>, ''m''<sub>2</sub>, ..., ''m<sub>N</sub>'', each particle has a [[position vector]], denoted '''r'''<sub>1</sub>, '''r'''<sub>2</sub>, ..., '''r'''<sub>''N''</sub>. [[Cartesian coordinates]] are often sufficient, so {{nowrap|1='''r'''<sub>1</sub> = (''x''<sub>1</sub>, ''y''<sub>1</sub>, ''z''<sub>1</sub>)}}, {{nowrap|1='''r'''<sub>2</sub> = (''x''<sub>2</sub>, ''y''<sub>2</sub>, ''z''<sub>2</sub>)}} and so on. In [[three-dimensional space]], each position vector requires three [[coordinate vector|coordinates]] to uniquely define the location of a point, so there are 3''N'' coordinates to uniquely define the configuration of the system. These are all specific points in space to locate the particles; a general point in space is written {{nowrap|1='''r''' = (''x'', ''y'', ''z'')}}. The [[velocity]] of each particle is how fast the particle moves along its path of motion, and is the [[time derivative]] of its position, thus
<math display="block">
 \mathbf{v}_1 = \frac{d\mathbf{r}_1}{dt},
 \mathbf{v}_2 = \frac{d\mathbf{r}_2}{dt},
 \ldots,
 \mathbf{v}_N = \frac{d\mathbf{r}_N}{dt}.
</math>
In Newtonian mechanics, the [[equations of motion]] are given by [[Newton's laws]]. The second law "net [[force]] equals mass times [[acceleration]]",
<math display="block">
 \sum \mathbf{F} = m \frac{d^2\mathbf{r}}{dt^2},
</math>
applies to each particle. For an ''N''-particle system in 3 dimensions, there are 3''N'' second-degree [[ordinary differential equation]]s in the positions of the particles to solve for.

=== Lagrangian ===
Instead of forces, Lagrangian mechanics uses the [[energy|energies]] in the system. The central quantity of Lagrangian mechanics is the '''Lagrangian''', a function which summarizes the dynamics of the entire system. Overall, the Lagrangian has units of energy, but no single expression for all physical systems. Any function which generates the correct equations of motion, in agreement with physical laws, can be taken as a Lagrangian. It is nevertheless possible to construct general expressions for large classes of applications. The ''non-relativistic'' Lagrangian for a system of particles in the absence of an electromagnetic field is given by<ref>{{harvnb|Torby|1984|page=270}}</ref>
<math display="block">
 L = T - V,
</math>
where
<math display="block">
 T = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{k=1}^N m_k v^2_k
</math>
is the total [[kinetic energy]] of the system, equaling the [[summation|sum]] Σ of the kinetic energies of the <math>N</math> particles. Each particle labeled <math>k</math> has mass <math>m_k,</math> and {{nowrap|1=''v''<sub>''k''</sub><sup>2</sup> = '''v'''<sub>''k''</sub> · '''v'''<sub>''k''</sub>}} is the magnitude squared of its velocity, equivalent to the [[dot product]] of the velocity with itself.<ref name="Torby 1984 page=269">{{harvnb|Torby|1984|page=269}}</ref>

Kinetic energy {{nowrap|1=''T''}} is the energy of the system's motion and is a function only of the velocities '''v'''<sub>''k''</sub>, not the positions '''r'''<sub>''k''</sub>, nor time ''t'', so {{nowrap|1=''T'' = ''T''('''v'''<sub>1</sub>, '''v'''<sub>2</sub>, ...).}}

''V'', the [[potential energy]] of the system, reflects the energy of interaction between the particles, i.e. how much energy any one particle has due to all the others, together with any external influences. For [[conservative force]]s (e.g. [[Newtonian gravity]]), it is a function of the position vectors of the particles only, so {{nowrap|1=''V'' = ''V''('''r'''<sub>1</sub>, '''r'''<sub>2</sub>, ...).}} For those non-conservative forces which can be derived from an appropriate potential (e.g. [[electromagnetic potential]]), the velocities will appear also, {{nowrap|1=''V'' = ''V''('''r'''<sub>1</sub>, '''r'''<sub>2</sub>, ..., '''v'''<sub>1</sub>, '''v'''<sub>2</sub>, ...).}} If there is some external field or external driving force changing with time, the potential changes with time, so most generally {{nowrap|1=''V'' = ''V''('''r'''<sub>1</sub>, '''r'''<sub>2</sub>, ..., '''v'''<sub>1</sub>, '''v'''<sub>2</sub>, ..., ''t'').}}

=== Mathematical formulation (for finite particle systems) ===

An equivalent but more mathematically formal definition of the Lagrangian is as follows.<ref>{{cite book
 | last1 = Cortés
 | first1 = Vicente
 | last2 = Haupt
 | first2 = Alexander S.
 | title = Mathematical Methods of Classical Physics
 | publisher = Springer
 | year = 2023
 | chapter = 2
 | url = https://arxiv.org/pdf/1612.03100
 | arxiv = 1612.03100
 | access-date = 2025-06-24
}}</ref>  
For  a system of ''N'' particles in three-dimensional space, the [[configuration space (physics)|configuration space]] of the system is a smooth manifold <math>Q \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{3N}</math>, where each configuration <math> q \in Q </math> specifies the spatial positions of each of the particles at a given instant of time, and the manifold is composed of all the configurations that are allowed by the constraints on the system.

The Lagrangian is a smooth function:
<math>L : TQ \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R},</math>
where <math>TQ \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{6N}</math> is the [[tangent bundle]] of the configuration space. That is, each element in <math>TQ</math> represents both the positions and the velocities of the particles, and can be written as a tuple <math>(q_1,\ldots, q_N,\dot q_1,\ldots \dot q_N)</math> with <math>q_i</math> and <math>\dot q_i</math> specifying a position and a velocity of the i'th particle respectively. The time dependence <math>t \in \mathbb{R}</math> allows for the Lagrangian to describe time-dependent forces or potentials.

A [[trajectory]] of the system is a smooth function
<math>q : [t_0, t_1] \to Q,</math>
describing the evolution of the configuration over time. Its velocity is the time derivative <math>\dot{q}(t) \in T_{q(t)}Q</math> of <math>q(t)</math>, and the pair <math>(q(t),\dot q(t)) \in TQ</math> is  thus an element of the bundle for any <math>t</math>. The [[action functional]] of the trajectory can therefore be defined as the integral of the Lagrangian along the path:
<math>S[q] = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} L(q(t), \dot{q}(t), t) \, dt.</math>

The laws of motion in Lagrangian mechanics are derived from the postulate that among all trajectories between two given configurations, the actual one that will be taken by the system must be a critical point (often but not necessarily a local minimum) of the action functional. This leads to the [[Euler–Lagrange equation]]s (see also below).

== Equations of motion ==

For a system of particles with masses <math>m_1, \ldots, m_N</math>, the [[kinetic energy]] is:
<math>T(q, \dot{q}) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^N m_i \|\dot{q}_i\|^2,</math>
where <math>\dot{q}_i \in \mathbb{R}^3</math> is the velocity of particle ''i''.

The [[potential energy]] <math>V(q, t)</math> depends only on the configuration (and possibly on time), and typically arises from conservative forces.

The standard ''Lagrangian'' is given by the difference:
<math>L(q, \dot{q}, t) = T(q, \dot{q}) - V(q, t).</math>

This formulation covers both conservative and time-dependent systems and forms the basis for generalizations to continuous systems (fields), constrained systems, and systems with curved configuration spaces.

If ''T'' or ''V'' or both depend explicitly on time due to time-varying constraints or external influences, the Lagrangian {{nowrap|1=''L''('''r'''<sub>1</sub>, '''r'''<sub>2</sub>, ... '''v'''<sub>1</sub>, '''v'''<sub>2</sub>, ... ''t'')}} is ''explicitly time-dependent''. If neither the potential nor the kinetic energy depend on time, then the Lagrangian {{nowrap|1=''L''('''r'''<sub>1</sub>, '''r'''<sub>2</sub>, ... '''v'''<sub>1</sub>, '''v'''<sub>2</sub>, ...)}} is ''explicitly independent of time''. In either case, the Lagrangian always has implicit time dependence through the generalized coordinates.

With these definitions, ''Lagrange's equations'' are<ref>{{harvnb|Hand|Finch|1998|page=60–61}}</ref>
{{Equation box 1
|indent =:
|title='''Lagrange's equations'''
|equation = <math>\frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{r}_k} - \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\mathbf{r}}_k} + \sum_{i=1}^C \lambda_i\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial \mathbf{r}_k} = 0,</math>
|cellpadding= 6
|border
|border colour = #0073CF
|background colour=#F5FFFA}}
where ''k'' = 1, 2, ..., ''N'' labels the particles, there is a [[Lagrange multiplier]] ''λ<sub>i</sub>'' for each constraint equation ''f''<sub>''i''</sub>, and
<math display="block">
 \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{r}_k} \equiv \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_k}, \frac{\partial}{\partial y_k}, \frac{\partial}{\partial z_k}\right), \quad
 \frac{\partial}{\partial \dot{\mathbf{r}}_k} \equiv \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial \dot{x}_k}, \frac{\partial}{\partial \dot{y}_k}, \frac{\partial}{\partial \dot{z}_k}\right)
</math>
are each shorthands for a vector of [[partial derivative]]s {{math|∂/∂}} with respect to the indicated variables (not a derivative with respect to the entire vector).<ref group="nb">Sometimes in this context the [[variational derivative]] denoted and defined as
<math display="block">
 \frac{\delta}{\delta \mathbf{r}_k} \equiv \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{r}_k} - \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{\partial}{\partial \dot{\mathbf{r}}_k}
</math>
is used. Throughout this article only partial and total derivatives are used.</ref> Each overdot is a shorthand for a [[time derivative]]. This procedure does increase the number of equations to solve compared to Newton's laws, from 3''N'' to {{nowrap|3''N'' + ''C''}}, because there are 3''N'' coupled second-order differential equations in the position coordinates and multipliers, plus ''C'' constraint equations. However, when solved alongside the position coordinates of the particles, the multipliers can yield information about the constraint forces. The coordinates do not need to be eliminated by solving the constraint equations.

In the Lagrangian, the position coordinates and velocity components are all [[Dependent and independent variables#In pure mathematics|independent variables]], and derivatives of the Lagrangian are taken with respect to these separately according to the usual [[differentiation rules]] (e.g. the partial derivative of ''L'' with respect to the ''z'' velocity component of particle&nbsp;2, defined by {{nowrap|1=''v''<sub>''z'',2</sub> = ''dz''<sub>2</sub>/''dt''}}, is just {{nowrap|∂''L''/∂''v''<sub>''z'',2</sub>}}; no awkward [[chain rule]]s or total derivatives need to be used to relate the velocity component to the corresponding coordinate ''z''<sub>2</sub>).

In each constraint equation, one coordinate is redundant because it is determined from the other coordinates. The number of ''independent'' coordinates is therefore {{nowrap|1=''n'' = 3''N'' − ''C''}}. We can transform each position vector to a common set of ''n'' [[generalized coordinates]], conveniently written as an ''n''-tuple {{nowrap|1='''q''' = (''q''<sub>1</sub>, ''q''<sub>2</sub>, ... ''q<sub>n</sub>'')}}, by expressing each position vector, and hence the position coordinates, as [[function (mathematics)|functions]] of the generalized coordinates and time:
<math display="block">
 \mathbf{r}_k = \mathbf{r}_k(\mathbf{q}, t) = \big(x_k(\mathbf{q}, t), y_k(\mathbf{q}, t), z_k(\mathbf{q}, t), t\big).
</math>

The vector '''q''' is a point in the [[Configuration space (physics)|configuration space]] of the system. The time derivatives of the generalized coordinates are called the generalized velocities, and for each particle the transformation of its velocity vector, the [[total derivative]] of its position with respect to time, is
<math display="block">
 \dot{q}_j = \frac{\mathrm{d}q_j}{\mathrm{d}t}, \quad
 \mathbf{v}_k = \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_k}{\partial q_j}\dot{q}_j + \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_k}{\partial t}.
</math>

Given this '''v'''<sub>''k''</sub>, the kinetic energy ''in generalized coordinates'' depends on the generalized velocities, generalized coordinates, and time if the position vectors depend explicitly on time due to time-varying constraints, so <math>T = T(\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}}, t).</math>

With these definitions, the [[Euler–Lagrange equation]]s,<ref>{{harvnb|Penrose|2007|page=}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Hand|Finch|1998|page=19}}</ref>
{{Equation box 1
|indent =:
|title=Lagrange's equations 
|equation = <math>\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} \left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_j} \right) =  \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_j}</math>
|cellpadding
|border
|border colour = #0073CF
|background colour=#F5FFFA}}
are mathematical results from the [[calculus of variations]], which can also be used in mechanics. Substituting in the Lagrangian {{nowrap|1=''L''('''q''', d'''q'''/d''t'', ''t'')}} gives the [[equations of motion]] of the system. The number of equations has decreased compared to Newtonian mechanics, from 3''N'' to {{nowrap|1=''n'' = 3''N'' − ''C''}} coupled second-order differential equations in the generalized coordinates. These equations do not include constraint forces at all, only non-constraint forces need to be accounted for.

Although the equations of motion include [[partial derivative]]s, the results of the partial derivatives are still [[ordinary differential equation]]s in the position coordinates of the particles. The [[total derivative|total time derivative]] denoted d/d''t'' often involves [[implicit differentiation]]. Both equations are linear in the Lagrangian, but generally are nonlinear coupled equations in the coordinates.

=== Extensions ===
As already noted, this form of ''L'' is applicable to many important classes of system, but not everywhere. For [[relativistic Lagrangian mechanics]] it must be replaced as a whole by a function consistent with special relativity (scalar under Lorentz transformations) or general relativity (4-scalar).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cremaschini |first1=Claudio |last2=Tessarotto |first2=Massimo |date=2015-06-30 |title=Synchronous Lagrangian variational principles in General Relativity |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1140/epjp/i2015-15123-4 |journal=The European Physical Journal Plus |language=en |volume=130 |issue=6 |page=123 |doi=10.1140/epjp/i2015-15123-4 |arxiv=1609.04418 |bibcode=2015EPJP..130..123C |issn=2190-5444}}</ref> Where a magnetic field is present, the expression for the potential energy needs restating.{{Citation needed|date=September 2024}} And for dissipative forces (e.g., [[friction]]), another function must be introduced alongside Lagrangian often referred to as a "[[Rayleigh dissipation function]]" to account for the loss of energy.<ref>Bersani AM, Caressa P. Lagrangian descriptions of dissipative systems: a review. ''Mathematics and Mechanics of Solids''. 2021;26(6):785-803. Doi: 10.1177/1081286520971834</ref>

One or more of the particles may each be subject to one or more [[holonomic constraints]]; such a constraint is described by an equation of the form {{nowrap|1=''f''('''r''', ''t'') = 0.}} If the number of constraints in the system is ''C'', then each constraint has an equation {{nowrap|1=''f''<sub>1</sub>('''r''', ''t'') = 0,}} {{nowrap|1=''f''<sub>2</sub>('''r''', ''t'') = 0,}} ..., {{nowrap|1=''f<sub>C</sub>''('''r''', ''t'') = 0,}} each of which could apply to any of the particles. If particle ''k'' is subject to constraint ''i'', then {{nowrap|1=''f<sub>i</sub>''('''r'''<sub>''k''</sub>, ''t'') = 0.}} At any instant of time, the coordinates of a constrained particle are linked together and not independent. The constraint equations determine the allowed paths the particles can move along, but not where they are or how fast they go at every instant of time. [[Nonholonomic constraints]] depend on the particle velocities, accelerations, or higher derivatives of position. Lagrangian mechanics can only be applied to systems whose constraints, if any, are all holonomic. Three examples of nonholonomic constraints are:<ref>{{harvnb|Hand|Finch|1998|page=36–40}}</ref> when the constraint equations are non-integrable, when the constraints have inequalities, or when the constraints involve complicated non-conservative forces like friction. Nonholonomic constraints require special treatment, and one may have to revert to [[Newton's laws of motion|Newtonian mechanics]] or use other methods.<ref>{{Citation |last=Pfeiffer |first=Friedrich |chapter=Constraint Systems |date=2008 |title=Mechanical System Dynamics |series=Lecture Notes in Applied and Computational Mechanics |volume=40 |pages=85–186 |editor-last=Pfeiffer |editor-first=Friedrich |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-540-79436-3_3 |access-date=2024-09-23 |place=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-79436-3_3 |isbn=978-3-540-79436-3|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== From Newtonian to Lagrangian mechanics ==

=== Newton's laws ===
[[File:GodfreyKneller-IsaacNewton-1689.jpg|thumb|upright=0.7|[[Isaac Newton]] (1642–1727)]]

For simplicity, Newton's laws can be illustrated for one particle without much loss of generality (for a system of ''N'' particles, all of these equations apply to each particle in the system). The [[equation of motion]] for a particle of constant mass ''m'' is [[Newton's second law]] of 1687, in modern vector notation
<math display="block">
 \mathbf{F} = m \mathbf{a},
</math>
where '''a''' is its acceleration and '''F''' the resultant force acting ''on'' it. Where the mass is varying, the equation needs to be generalised to take the time derivative of the momentum. In three spatial dimensions, this is a system of three coupled second-order [[ordinary differential equation]]s to solve, since there are three components in this vector equation. The solution is the position vector '''r''' of the particle at time ''t'', subject to the [[initial condition]]s of '''r''' and '''v''' when {{nowrap|1=''t'' = 0.}}

Newton's laws are easy to use in Cartesian coordinates, but Cartesian coordinates are not always convenient, and for other coordinate systems the equations of motion can become complicated. In a set of [[curvilinear coordinates]] {{nowrap|1='''''ξ''''' = (''ξ''<sup>1</sup>, ''ξ''<sup>2</sup>, ''ξ''<sup>3</sup>),}} the law in [[tensor index notation]] is the ''"Lagrangian form"''<ref name="Kay 1988">{{harvnb|Kay|page=156|1988}}</ref><ref name="Synge 1949">{{harvnb|Synge|Schild|page=150–152|1949}}</ref>
<math display="block">
 F^a = m \left( \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 \xi^a}{\mathrm{d}t^2} + \Gamma^a{}_{bc} \frac{\mathrm{d}\xi^b}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{\mathrm{d}\xi^c}{\mathrm{d}t} \right) = g^{ak} \left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} \frac{\partial T}{\partial \dot{\xi}^k} - \frac{\partial T}{\partial \xi^k}\right), \quad
 \dot{\xi}^a \equiv \frac{\mathrm{d} \xi^a }{\mathrm{d}t},
</math>
where ''F''<sup>''a''</sup> is the ''a''-th [[Covariance and contravariance of vectors|contravariant component]] of the resultant force acting on the particle, Γ<sup>''a''</sup><sub>''bc''</sub> are the [[Christoffel symbols]] of the second kind,
<math display="block">
 T = \frac{1}{2} m g_{bc} \frac{\mathrm{d} \xi^b}{\mathrm{d}t} \frac{\mathrm{d} \xi^c}{\mathrm{d}t}
</math>
is the kinetic energy of the particle, and ''g<sub>bc</sub>'' the [[Covariance and contravariance of vectors|covariant components]] of the ''[[metric tensor]]'' of the curvilinear coordinate system. All the indices ''a'', ''b'', ''c'', each take the values 1, 2, 3. Curvilinear coordinates are not the same as generalized coordinates.

It may seem like an overcomplication to cast Newton's law in this form, but there are advantages. The acceleration components in terms of the Christoffel symbols can be avoided by evaluating derivatives of the kinetic energy instead. If there is no resultant force acting on the particle, {{nowrap|1='''F''' = '''0''',}} it does not accelerate, but moves with constant velocity in a straight line. Mathematically, the solutions of the differential equation are ''[[geodesic]]s'', the curves of extremal length between two points in space (these may end up being minimal, that is the shortest paths, but not necessarily). In flat 3D real space the geodesics are simply straight lines. So for a free particle, Newton's second law coincides with the geodesic equation and states that free particles follow geodesics, the extremal trajectories it can move along. If the particle is subject to forces {{nowrap|'''F''' ≠ '''0''',}} the particle accelerates due to forces acting on it and deviates away from the geodesics it would follow if free. With appropriate extensions of the quantities given here in flat 3D space to 4D [[curved spacetime]], the above form of Newton's law also carries over to [[Albert Einstein|Einstein]]'s [[general relativity]], in which case free particles follow geodesics in curved spacetime that are no longer "straight lines" in the ordinary sense.<ref>{{harvnb|Foster|Nightingale|1995|page=89}}</ref>

However, we still need to know the total resultant force '''F''' acting on the particle, which in turn requires the resultant non-constraint force '''N''' plus the resultant constraint force '''C''',
<math display="block">
 \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{C} + \mathbf{N}.
</math>

The constraint forces can be complicated, since they generally depend on time. Also, if there are constraints, the curvilinear coordinates are not independent but related by one or more constraint equations.

The constraint forces can either be eliminated from the equations of motion, so only the non-constraint forces remain, or included by including the constraint equations in the equations of motion.

=== D'Alembert's principle ===
[[File:Maurice Quentin de La Tour - Portrait de Jean Le Rond d'Alembert.jpg|thumb|upright=0.7|[[Jean d'Alembert]] (1717–1783)]]

{{multiple image
|align = vertical
|width = 200
|image1 = Constraint force virtual displacement 1 dof.svg
|caption1 = One degree of freedom.
|image2 = Constraint force virtual displacement 2 dof.svg
|caption2 = Two degrees of freedom.
|footer = Constraint force '''C''' and virtual displacement ''δ'''''r''' for a particle of mass ''m'' confined to a curve. The resultant non-constraint force is '''N'''.}}

A fundamental result in [[analytical mechanics]] is [[D'Alembert's principle]], introduced in 1708 by [[Jacques Bernoulli]] to understand [[static equilibrium]], and developed by [[D'Alembert]] in 1743 to solve dynamical problems.<ref>{{harvnb|Hand|Finch|1998|page=4}}</ref> The principle asserts for ''N'' particles the virtual work, i.e. the work along a virtual displacement, <math>\delta \mathbf{r}_k</math>, is zero:<ref name="Torby 1984 page=269"/>
<math display="block">\sum_{k=1}^N ( \mathbf {N}_k + \mathbf {C}_k - m_k \mathbf{a}_k )\cdot \delta \mathbf{r}_k = 0.</math>

The ''[[virtual displacement]]s'', <math>\delta \mathbf{r}_k</math>, are by definition infinitesimal changes in the configuration of the system consistent with the constraint forces acting on the system ''at an instant of time'',<ref name="Goldstein 1980 page=16–18">{{harvnb|Goldstein|1980|pages=16–18}}</ref> i.e. in such a way that the constraint forces maintain the constrained motion. They are not the same as the actual displacements in the system, which are caused by the resultant constraint and non-constraint forces acting on the particle to accelerate and move it.<ref group=nb>Here the virtual displacements are assumed reversible, it is possible for some systems to have non-reversible virtual displacements that violate this principle, see [[Udwadia–Kalaba equation]].</ref> [[Virtual work]] is the work done along a virtual displacement for any force (constraint or non-constraint).

Since the constraint forces act perpendicular to the motion of each particle in the system to maintain the constraints, the total virtual work by the constraint forces acting on the system is zero:<ref name="Hand 1998 page=15">{{harvnb|Hand|Finch|1998|page=15}}</ref><ref group="nb">In other words
<math display="block">\mathbf{C}_k\cdot\delta\mathbf{r}_k = 0</math>
for particle ''k'' subject to a constraint force, however
<math display="block">C_{k\,x} \delta x_k \neq 0,\quad C_{k\,y} \delta y_k \neq 0,\quad C_{k\,z} \delta z_k \neq 0</math>
because of the constraint equations on the '''r'''<sub>''k''</sub> coordinates.</ref>
<math display="block">\sum_{k=1}^N \mathbf {C}_k \cdot \delta \mathbf{r}_k = 0,</math>
so that
<math display="block">\sum_{k=1}^N (\mathbf {N}_k - m_k \mathbf{a}_k ) \cdot \delta \mathbf{r}_k = 0.</math>

Thus D'Alembert's principle allows us to concentrate on only the applied non-constraint forces, and exclude the constraint forces in the equations of motion.<ref name="Hand 1998 page=15"/><ref>{{harvnb|Fetter|Walecka|1980|page=53}}</ref> The form shown is also independent of the choice of coordinates. However, it cannot be readily used to set up the equations of motion in an arbitrary coordinate system since the displacements <math>\delta \mathbf{r}_k</math> might be connected by a constraint equation, which prevents us from setting the ''N'' individual summands to 0. We will therefore seek a system of mutually independent coordinates for which the total sum will be 0 if and only if the individual summands are 0. Setting each of the summands to 0 will eventually give us our separated equations of motion.

=== Equations of motion from D'Alembert's principle ===
If there are constraints on particle ''k'', then since the coordinates of the position {{nowrap|1='''r'''<sub>''k''</sub> = (''x''<sub>''k''</sub>, ''y''<sub>''k''</sub>, ''z''<sub>''k''</sub>)}} are linked together by a constraint equation, so are those of the [[virtual displacement]]s {{nowrap|1=''δ'''''r'''<sub>''k''</sub> = (''δx''<sub>''k''</sub>, ''δy''<sub>''k''</sub>, ''δz''<sub>''k''</sub>)}}. Since the generalized coordinates are independent, we can avoid the complications with the ''δ'''''r'''<sub>''k''</sub> by converting to virtual displacements in the generalized coordinates. These are related in the same form as a [[total differential]],<ref name="Torby 1984 page=269"/>
<math display="block">\delta \mathbf{r}_k = \sum_{j=1}^n \frac {\partial \mathbf{r}_k} {\partial q_j} \delta q_j.</math>

There is no partial time derivative with respect to time multiplied by a time increment, since this is a virtual displacement, one along the constraints in an ''instant'' of time.

The first term in D'Alembert's principle above is the virtual work done by the non-constraint forces '''N'''<sub>''k''</sub> along the virtual displacements ''δ'''''r'''<sub>''k''</sub>, and can without loss of generality be converted into the generalized analogues by the definition of [[generalized force]]s
<math display="block">Q_j = \sum_{k=1}^N \mathbf {N}_k \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_k}{\partial q_j},</math>
so that
<math display="block">\sum_{k=1}^N \mathbf{N}_k \cdot \delta \mathbf{r}_k = \sum_{k=1}^N  \mathbf {N}_k \cdot \sum_{j=1}^n \frac {\partial \mathbf{r}_k} {\partial q_j} \delta q_j = \sum_{j=1}^n Q_j \delta q_j.</math>

This is half of the conversion to generalized coordinates. It remains to convert the acceleration term into generalized coordinates, which is not immediately obvious. Recalling the Lagrange form of Newton's second law, the partial derivatives of the kinetic energy with respect to the generalized coordinates and velocities can be found to give the desired result:<ref name="Torby 1984 page=269"/>
<math display="block">\sum_{k=1}^N m_k \mathbf{a}_k \cdot \frac {\partial \mathbf{r}_k}{\partial q_j} = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{\partial T}{\partial \dot{q}_j} - \frac{\partial T}{\partial q_j}.</math>

Now D'Alembert's principle is in the generalized coordinates as required,
<math display="block">\sum_{j=1}^n \left[ Q_j - \left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{\partial T}{\partial \dot{q}_j} - \frac{\partial T}{\partial q_j} \right) \right] \delta q_j = 0, </math>
and since these virtual displacements ''δq''<sub>''j''</sub> are independent and nonzero, the coefficients can be equated to zero, resulting in Lagrange's equations<ref>{{harvnb|Kibble |Berkshire|edition=5th|2004|page=234}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Fetter|Walecka|1980|page=56}}</ref> or the  ''generalized equations of motion'',<ref>{{harvnb|Hand|Finch|1998|page=17}}</ref>
<math display="block">Q_j = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{\partial T}{\partial \dot{q}_j} - \frac{\partial T}{\partial q_j} </math>

These equations are equivalent to Newton's laws ''for the non-constraint forces''. The generalized forces in this equation are derived from the non-constraint forces only – the constraint forces have been excluded from D'Alembert's principle and do not need to be found. The generalized forces may be non-conservative, provided they satisfy D'Alembert's principle.<ref>{{harvnb|Hand|Finch|1998|page=15–17}}</ref>

=== Euler–Lagrange equations and Hamilton's principle ===
[[File:Least action principle.svg|250px|thumb|As the system evolves, '''q''' traces a path through [[configuration space (physics)|configuration space]] (only some are shown). The path taken by the system (red) has a stationary action (δ''S'' = 0) under small changes in the configuration of the system (δ'''q''').<ref name=penrose>{{cite book |author=R. Penrose| title=[[The Road to Reality]]| publisher= Vintage books| year=2007 | page = 474|isbn=978-0-679-77631-4}}</ref>]]

For a non-conservative force which depends on velocity, it ''may'' be possible to find a potential energy function ''V'' that depends on positions and velocities. If the generalized forces ''Q''<sub>''i''</sub> can be derived from a potential ''V'' such that<ref>{{harvnb|Goldstein|1980|page=23}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Kibble|Berkshire|edition=5th|2004|page=234–235}}</ref>
<math display="block">Q_j = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{\partial V}{\partial \dot{q}_j} - \frac{\partial V}{\partial q_j},</math>
equating to Lagrange's equations and defining the Lagrangian as {{nowrap|1=''L'' = ''T'' − ''V''}} obtains ''Lagrange's equations of the second kind'' or the [[Euler–Lagrange equation]]s of motion
<math display="block"> \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_j} - \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_j}  = 0. </math>

However, the Euler–Lagrange equations can only account for non-conservative forces ''if'' a potential can be found as shown. This may not always be possible for non-conservative forces, and Lagrange's equations do not involve any potential, only generalized forces; therefore they are more general than the Euler–Lagrange equations.

The Euler–Lagrange equations also follow from the [[calculus of variations]]. The ''variation'' of the Lagrangian is
<math display="block">\delta L = \sum_{j=1}^n \left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_j} \delta q_j + \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_j} \delta \dot{q}_j \right),\quad \delta \dot{q}_j \equiv \delta\frac{\mathrm{d}q_j}{\mathrm{d}t} \equiv \frac{\mathrm{d}(\delta q_j)}{\mathrm{d}t}, </math>
which has a form similar to the [[total differential]] of ''L'', but the virtual displacements and their time derivatives replace differentials, and there is no time increment in accordance with the definition of the virtual displacements. An [[integration by parts]] with respect to time can transfer the time derivative of ''δq''<sub>''j''</sub> to the ∂''L''/∂(d''q<sub>j</sub>''/d''t''), in the process exchanging d(''δq''<sub>''j''</sub>)/d''t'' for ''δq''<sub>''j''</sub>, allowing the independent virtual displacements to be factorized from the derivatives of the Lagrangian,
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\int_{t_1}^{t_2} \delta L \, \mathrm{d}t & =\int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sum_{j=1}^n \left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_j}\delta q_j +\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} \left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_j}\delta q_j\right) - \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_j}\delta q_j \right) \, \mathrm{d}t
\\ &= \sum_{j=1}^n\left[\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_j}\delta q_j\right]_{t_1}^{t_2} + \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sum_{j=1}^n \left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_j} - \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_j} \right)\delta q_j \, \mathrm{d}t.
\end{align} </math>

Now, if the condition {{nowrap|1=''δq''<sub>''j''</sub>(''t''<sub>1</sub>) = ''δq''<sub>''j''</sub>(''t''<sub>2</sub>) = 0}} holds for all ''j'', the terms not integrated are zero. If in addition the entire time integral of ''δL'' is zero, then because the ''δq''<sub>''j''</sub> are independent, and the only way for a definite integral to be zero is if the integrand equals zero, each of the coefficients of ''δq''<sub>''j''</sub> must also be zero. Then we obtain the equations of motion. This can be summarized by [[Hamilton's principle]] :
<math display="block">\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\delta L \, \mathrm{d}t = 0. </math>

The time integral of the Lagrangian is another quantity called the [[action (physics)|action]], defined as<ref>{{harvnb|Hand|Finch|1998|page=51}}</ref>
<math display="block">S = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} L\,\mathrm{d}t,</math>
which is a ''[[Functional (mathematics)|functional]]''; it takes in the Lagrangian function for all times between ''t''<sub>1</sub> and ''t''<sub>2</sub> and returns a scalar value. Its dimensions are the same as {{bracket|[[angular momentum]]}}, {{bracket|energy}}·{{bracket|time}}, or {{bracket|length}}·{{bracket|momentum}}. With this definition Hamilton's principle is
<math display="block">\delta S = 0. </math>

Instead of thinking about particles accelerating in response to applied forces, one might think of them picking out the path with a stationary action, with the end points of the path in configuration space held fixed at the initial and final times. Hamilton's principle is one of several [[action principles]].<ref name=HancTaylorTuleja>{{Cite journal |last1=Hanc |first1=Jozef |last2=Taylor |first2=Edwin F. |last3=Tuleja |first3=Slavomir |date=2005-07-01 |title=Variational mechanics in one and two dimensions |url=https://pubs.aip.org/ajp/article/73/7/603/1056166/Variational-mechanics-in-one-and-two-dimensions |journal=American Journal of Physics |language=en |volume=73 |issue=7 |pages=603–610 |doi=10.1119/1.1848516 |bibcode=2005AmJPh..73..603H |issn=0002-9505|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Historically, the idea of finding the shortest path a particle can follow subject to a force motivated the first applications of the [[calculus of variations]] to mechanical problems, such as the [[Brachistochrone problem]] solved by [[Jean Bernoulli]] in 1696, as well as [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz|Leibniz]], [[Daniel Bernoulli]], [[Guillaume de l'Hôpital|L'Hôpital]] around the same time, and [[Isaac Newton|Newton]] the following year.<ref name="Hand 1998 page=44–45">{{harvnb|Hand|Finch|1998|page=44–45}}</ref> Newton himself was thinking along the lines of the variational calculus, but did not publish.<ref name="Hand 1998 page=44–45"/> These ideas in turn lead to the [[variational principle]]s of mechanics, of [[Pierre de Fermat|Fermat]], [[Pierre Louis Maupertuis|Maupertuis]], [[Leonhard Euler|Euler]], [[William Rowan Hamilton|Hamilton]], and others.

Hamilton's principle can be applied to [[nonholonomic constraints]] if the constraint equations can be put into a certain form, a [[linear combination]] of first order differentials in the coordinates. The resulting constraint equation can be rearranged into first order differential equation.<ref>{{harvnb|Goldstein|1980}}</ref> This will not be given here.

=== Lagrange multipliers and constraints ===

The Lagrangian ''L'' can be varied in the Cartesian '''r'''<sub>''k''</sub> coordinates, for ''N'' particles,
<math display="block">\int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sum_{k=1}^N \left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{r}_k} - \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\mathbf{r}}_k} \right)\cdot\delta \mathbf{r}_k \, \mathrm{d}t = 0. </math>

Hamilton's principle is still valid even if the coordinates ''L'' is expressed in are not independent, here '''r'''<sub>''k''</sub>, but the constraints are still assumed to be holonomic.<ref>{{harvnb|Fetter|Walecka|1980|pp=68–70}}</ref> As always the end points are fixed {{nowrap|1=''δ'''''r'''<sub>''k''</sub>(''t''<sub>1</sub>) = ''δ'''''r'''<sub>''k''</sub>(''t''<sub>2</sub>) = '''0'''}} for all ''k''. What cannot be done is to simply equate the coefficients of ''δ'''''r'''<sub>''k''</sub> to zero because the ''δ'''''r'''<sub>''k''</sub> are not independent. Instead, the method of [[Lagrange multiplier]]s can be used to include the constraints. Multiplying each constraint equation {{nowrap|1=''f''<sub>''i''</sub>('''r'''<sub>''k''</sub>, ''t'') = 0}} by a Lagrange multiplier ''λ''<sub>''i''</sub> for ''i'' = 1, 2, ..., ''C'', and adding the results to the original Lagrangian, gives the new Lagrangian
<math display="block">L' = L(\mathbf{r}_1,\mathbf{r}_2,\ldots,\dot{\mathbf{r}}_1,\dot{\mathbf{r}}_2,\ldots,t) + \sum_{i=1}^C \lambda_i(t) f_i(\mathbf{r}_k,t). </math>

The Lagrange multipliers are arbitrary functions of time ''t'', but not functions of the coordinates '''r'''<sub>''k''</sub>, so the multipliers are on equal footing with the position coordinates. Varying this new Lagrangian and integrating with respect to time gives
<math display="block">\int_{t_1}^{t_2} \delta L' \mathrm{d}t = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sum_{k=1}^N \left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{r}_k} - \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\mathbf{r}}_k} + \sum_{i=1}^C \lambda_i \frac{\partial f_i }{\partial \mathbf{r}_k}\right)\cdot\delta \mathbf{r}_k \, \mathrm{d}t = 0. </math>

The introduced multipliers can be found so that the coefficients of ''δ'''''r'''<sub>''k''</sub> are zero, even though the '''r'''<sub>''k''</sub> are not independent. The equations of motion follow. From the preceding analysis, obtaining the solution to this integral is equivalent to the statement
<math display="block">\frac{\partial L'}{\partial \mathbf{r}_k} - \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{\partial L'}{\partial \dot{\mathbf{r}}_k} = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{r}_k} - \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\mathbf{r}}_k} + \sum_{i=1}^C \lambda_i \frac{\partial f_i }{\partial \mathbf{r}_k} = 0, </math>
which are '''Lagrange's equations of the first kind'''. Also, the ''λ''<sub>''i''</sub> Euler-Lagrange equations for the new Lagrangian return the constraint equations
<math display="block">\frac{\partial L'}{\partial \lambda_i} - \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{\partial L'}{\partial \dot{\lambda}_i}  = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad f_i(\mathbf{r}_k,t) = 0. </math>

For the case of a conservative force given by the gradient of some potential energy ''V'', a function of the '''r'''<sub>k</sub> coordinates only, substituting the Lagrangian {{nowrap|1=''L'' = ''T'' − ''V''}} gives
<math display="block">\underbrace{ \frac{\partial T}{\partial \mathbf{r}_k} - \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{\partial T}{\partial \dot{\mathbf{r}}_k} }_{-\mathbf{F}_k} + \underbrace{ - \frac{\partial V}{\partial \mathbf{r}_k}}_{\mathbf{N}_k} + \sum_{i=1}^C \lambda_i \frac{\partial f_i}{\partial \mathbf{r}_k} = 0, </math>
and identifying the derivatives of kinetic energy as the (negative of the) resultant force, and the derivatives of the potential equaling the non-constraint force, it follows the constraint forces are
<math display="block">\mathbf{C}_k = \sum_{i=1}^C \lambda_i \frac{\partial f_i}{\partial \mathbf{r}_k}, </math>
thus giving the constraint forces explicitly in terms of the constraint equations and the Lagrange multipliers.

== Properties of the Lagrangian ==
=== Non-uniqueness ===

The Lagrangian of a given system is not unique. A Lagrangian ''L'' can be multiplied by a nonzero constant ''a'' and shifted by an arbitrary constant ''b'', and the new Lagrangian {{nowrap|1=''L''′ = ''aL'' + ''b''}} will describe the same motion as ''L''. If one restricts as above to trajectories '''q''' over a given time interval {{nowrap|1={{bracket|''t''<sub>st</sub>, ''t''<sub>fin</sub>}}}} and fixed end points {{nowrap|1=''P''<sub>st</sub> = '''q'''(''t''<sub>st</sub>)}} and {{nowrap|1=''P''<sub>fin</sub> = '''q'''(''t''<sub>fin</sub>)}}, then two Lagrangians describing the same system can differ by the "total time derivative" of a function {{nowrap|1=''f''('''q''', ''t'')}}:<ref name="Landau 1976 page=4">{{harvnb|Landau|Lifshitz|edition=3rd|1976|page=4}}</ref>
<math display="block">L'(\mathbf{q},\dot\mathbf{q},t) = L(\mathbf{q},\dot\mathbf{q},t) + \frac{\mathrm{d}f(\mathbf{q},t)}{\mathrm{d}t},</math>
where <math display="inline"> \frac{\mathrm{d}f(\mathbf{q},t)}{\mathrm{d}t}</math> means <math display="inline"> \frac{\partial f(\mathbf{q},t)}{\partial t}+\sum_i \frac{\partial f(\mathbf{q},t)}{\partial q_i} {\dot q}_i.</math>

Both Lagrangians ''L'' and ''L''′ produce the same equations of motion<ref>{{harvnb|Goldstein|Poole|Safko|2002|edition=3rd|page=21}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Lifshitz|1976|page=4}}</ref> since the corresponding actions ''S'' and ''S''′ are related via
<math display="block">\begin{align}
S'[\mathbf{q}] &= \int^{t_\text{fin}}_{t_\text{st}} L'(\mathbf{q}(t),\dot\mathbf{q}(t),t)\,dt \\
&= \int^{t_\text{fin}}_{t_\text{st}} L(\mathbf{q}(t),\dot\mathbf{q}(t),t)\,dt + \int^{t_\text{fin}}_{t_\text{st}} \frac{\mathrm{d}f(\mathbf{q}(t),t)}{\mathrm{d}t}\, dt \\
&=
S[\mathbf{q}] + f(P_\text{fin},t_\text{fin}) - f(P_\text{st},t_\text{st}),
\end{align}</math>
with the last two components {{nowrap|1=''f''(''P''<sub>fin</sub>, ''t''<sub>fin</sub>)}} and {{nowrap|1=''f''(''P''<sub>st</sub>, ''t''<sub>st</sub>)}} independent of '''q'''.

=== Invariance under point transformations ===

Given a set of generalized coordinates '''q''', if we change these variables to a new set of generalized coordinates '''Q''' according to a [[Canonical transformation|point transformation]] {{nowrap|1='''Q''' = '''Q'''('''q''', ''t'')}} which is invertible as {{nowrap|1='''q''' = '''q'''('''Q''', ''t'')}}, the new Lagrangian ''L''′ is a function of the new coordinates and similarly for the constraints
<math display="block">\begin{align}L'(\mathbf{Q}, \dot{\mathbf{Q}},t) &= L(\mathbf{q}(\mathbf{Q},t), \dot{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{Q},\dot{\mathbf{Q}},t), t ),\\
\phi_j'(\mathbf{Q},t)&=\phi_j(\mathbf{q}(\mathbf{Q},t),t)
\end{align}</math>
and by the [[chain rule#Higher dimensions|chain rule]] for partial differentiation, Lagrange's equations are invariant under this transformation;<ref>{{harvnb|Goldstein|1980|page=21}}</ref>{{Citation needed|date=February 2025|reason=better to have citation for proof including constraint, remove if unnecessary}}

<math display="block">\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{\partial L'}{\partial \dot{Q}_i} = \frac{\partial L'}{\partial Q_i}+\sum_j\lambda_j\frac{\partial \phi'_j}{\partial Q_i}.</math>{{math proof
| proof =
For a coordinate transformation <math>Q_i=Q_i(\mathbf q,t) </math>, we have
<math display="block">d{Q_i} =\sum_k\frac{\partial Q_i}{\partial q_k}d{q_k}+\frac{\partial Q_k}{\partial t} d t,</math>
which implies that <math>\dot{Q_i} =\sum_k\frac{\partial Q_i}{\partial q_k}(\mathbf q,t)\,\dot q_k+\frac{\partial Q_k}{\partial t}(\mathbf q,t)</math> which implies that <math>\frac{\partial \dot{Q_i}}{\partial \dot q_k}=\frac{\partial Q_i}{\partial q_k}</math>.

It also follows that:
<math display="block">\frac{\partial\dot{Q_i}}{\partial q_j} =\sum_k\frac{\partial^2 Q_i}{\partial q_j \partial q_k}(\mathbf q,t) \, \dot q_k+\frac{\partial^2 Q_k}{\partial q_j \partial t}(\mathbf q,t)</math>
and similarly:
<math display="block">\frac{d}{dt} \left(\frac{\partial {Q_i}}{\partial q_j} \right)=\sum_k\frac{\partial^2 Q_i}{\partial q_k \partial q_j}(\mathbf q,t) \, \dot q_k+\frac{\partial^2 Q_k}{\partial t \partial q_j}(\mathbf q,t)</math>
which imply that <math>\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\partial Q_i}{\partial q_k}\right)= \frac{\partial \dot Q_i}{\partial q_k}</math>. The two derived relations can be employed in the proof.

Starting from Euler Lagrange equations in initial set of generalized coordinates, we have:
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
\frac{d}{d t}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot{q}_{i}}-\frac{{\partial}L}{\partial q_{i}}-\sum_j\lambda_j\frac{\partial \phi_j}{\partial q_i}=0\\
\sum_k\left( \frac{d}{d t}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot{Q}_{k}}\frac{\partial \dot Q_k}{\partial\dot{q}_{i}}\right)-\frac{{\partial}L}{\partial Q_{k}}\frac{\partial  Q_k}{\partial{q}_{i}}-\frac{{\partial}L}{\partial \dot Q_{k}}\frac{\partial \dot Q_k}{\partial {q}_{i}}-\sum_j\lambda_j\frac{\partial \phi_j}{\partial Q_k}\frac{\partial Q_k}{\partial q_i}\right)=0\\
\sum_k\left( \frac{d}{d t}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot{Q}_{k}}\right)\frac{\partial \dot Q_k}{\partial\dot{q}_{i}}+ \frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot{Q}_{k}}\frac{d}{d t}\left(\frac{\partial \dot Q_k}{\partial\dot{q}_{i}}\right)-\frac{{\partial}L}{\partial Q_{k}}\frac{\partial  \dot Q_k}{\partial \dot {q}_{i}}-\frac{{\partial}L}{\partial \dot Q_{k}}\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\partial Q_k}{\partial q_i}\right) -\sum_j\lambda_j\frac{\partial \phi_j}{\partial Q_k}\frac{\partial Q_k}{\partial q_i}\right) = 0 \\
\sum_k \left(\frac{d}{d t}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot{Q}_{k}}\right)-\frac{\partial L}{\partial Q_k}-\sum_j\lambda_j\frac{\partial \phi_j}{\partial Q_k}\right)\frac{\partial Q_k}{\partial q_i}=0\\
\end{align}
</math>

Since the transformation from <math>q\rightarrow Q</math> is invertible, it follows that the form of the Euler-Lagrange equation is invariant i.e.,
<math display="block">
\frac{d}{d t}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot{Q}_{i}}-\frac{{\partial}L}{\partial Q_{i}}-\sum_j\lambda_j\frac{\partial \phi_j}{\partial Q_i}=0.
</math>
}}

=== Cyclic coordinates and conserved momenta ===

An important property of the Lagrangian is that [[Conservation law|conserved quantities]] can easily be read off from it. The ''generalized momentum'' "canonically conjugate to" the coordinate ''q<sub>i</sub>'' is defined by
<math display="block">p_i =\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_i}.</math>

If the Lagrangian ''L'' does ''not'' depend on some coordinate ''q<sub>i</sub>'', it follows immediately from the Euler–Lagrange equations that
<math display="block">\dot{p}_i = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_i} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i} = 0</math>
and integrating shows the corresponding generalized momentum equals a constant, a conserved quantity. This is a special case of [[Noether's theorem]]. Such coordinates are called "cyclic" or "ignorable".

For example, a system may have a Lagrangian
<math display="block">L(r,\theta,\dot{s},\dot{z},\dot{r},\dot{\theta},\dot{\phi},t),</math>
where ''r'' and ''z'' are lengths along straight lines, ''s'' is an arc length along some curve, and ''θ'' and ''φ'' are angles. Notice ''z'', ''s'', and ''φ'' are all absent in the Lagrangian even though their velocities are not. Then the momenta
<math display="block">p_z =\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot z},\quad p_s =\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot s},\quad p_\phi =\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot \phi},</math>
are all conserved quantities. The units and nature of each generalized momentum will depend on the corresponding coordinate; in this case ''p''<sub>''z''</sub> is a translational momentum in the ''z'' direction, ''p''<sub>''s''</sub> is also a translational momentum along the curve ''s'' is measured, and ''p''<sub>''φ''</sub> is an angular momentum in the plane the angle ''φ'' is measured in. However complicated the motion of the system is, all the coordinates and velocities will vary in such a way that these momenta are conserved.

=== Energy ===
Given a Lagrangian <math>L,</math> the [[Hamiltonian mechanics|Hamiltonian]] of the corresponding mechanical system is, by definition,
<math display="block">H = \biggl(\sum^n_{i=1} {\dot{q}}_i\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_i}\biggr) - L. </math>
This quantity will be equivalent to energy if the generalized coordinates are natural coordinates, i.e., they have no explicit time dependence when expressing position vector: <math>\mathbf{r}= \mathbf{r}(q_1, \cdots, q_n)</math>. From:
<math display="block">
T = \frac{m}{2}v^2 = \frac{m}{2} \sum_{i,j} \left(\frac{\partial \vec{r}}{\partial q_i} \dot{q}_i       \right)\cdot \left(\frac{\partial \vec{r}}{\partial q_j} \dot{q}_j\right) = \frac{m}{2} \sum_{i,j} a_{ij} \dot{q}_i\dot{q}_j
</math>
<math display="block">
\sum^n_{k=1} \dot{q}_k \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_k} = \sum^n_{k=1} \dot{q}_k \frac{\partial T}{\partial \dot{q}_k} = \frac{m}{2}\left( 2 \sum_{i,j} a_{ij} \dot{q}_i\dot{q}_j\right) = 2T
</math>
<math display="block">
H = \left(\sum^n_{i=1} {\dot{q}}_i\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_i}\right) - L = 2T - (T - V) = T + V = E
</math>
where <math>a_{ij}=\frac{\partial\mathbf r}{\partial q_i}\cdot \frac{\partial\mathbf r}{\partial q_j}</math> is a symmetric matrix that is defined for the derivation.

==== Invariance under coordinate transformations ====
At every time instant ''t'', the energy is invariant under [[Configuration space (physics)|configuration space]] coordinate changes {{nowrap|'''q''' → '''Q'''}}, i.e. (using natural coordinates)
<math display="block">E(\mathbf{q},\dot\mathbf{q},t) = E(\mathbf{Q},\dot\mathbf{Q},t).</math>
Besides this result, the proof below shows that, under such change of coordinates, the derivatives <math>\partial L/\partial {\dot q}_i</math> change as coefficients of a linear form.
{{math proof
| proof =
For a coordinate transformation {{nowrap|1='''Q''' = ''F''('''q''')}}, we have
<math display="block">d\mathbf{Q} = F_*(\mathbf{q})d\mathbf{q},</math>
where <math>F_*(\mathbf{q})</math> is the [[pushforward (differential)|tangent map]] of the vector space
<math display="block">\left\{\sum^n_{i=1}{\dot q}_i\cdot \left(\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial q_i}\right|_{\mathbf{q}}\right)\ \biggl|\ {\dot q}_i \in \mathbb{R}\right\}</math>
to the vector space
<math display="block">\left\{\sum^n_{i=1}{\dot Q}_i\cdot \left(\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial Q_i}\right|_{F(\mathbf{q})}\right)\ \biggl|\ {\dot Q}_i \in \mathbb{R}\right\},</math>
and
<math display="block">\textstyle F_*(\mathbf{q}) = \left(\left.\frac{\partial F_i}{\partial q_j}\right|_{\mathbf{q}}\right)^n_{i,j=1}</math>
is the Jacobian. In the coordinates <math>\dot q_i</math> and <math>\dot Q_i,</math> the previous formula for <math>d\mathbf{Q}</math> has the form <math>\dot \mathbf{Q} = F_*(\mathbf{q})\dot\mathbf{q}.</math> After differentiation involving the product rule,
<math display="block">d\dot \mathbf{Q} =  G(\mathbf{q},\dot\mathbf{q})d\mathbf{q} + F_*(\mathbf{q})d\dot\mathbf{q},</math>
where
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
G(\mathbf{q},\dot\mathbf{q})d\mathbf{q}
&\,\stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\, d(F_*(\mathbf{q}))\dot\mathbf{q}
= \left(\sum^n_{k=1}\frac{\partial^2 F_i}{\partial q_j \partial q_k}\biggl|_\mathbf{q} dq_k \right)^n_{i,j=1}{\dot \mathbf{q}}
= \left(\sum^n_{j=1}{\dot q}_j\sum^n_{k=1}\frac{\partial^2 F_i}{\partial q_j \partial q_k}\biggl|_\mathbf{q} dq_k \right)^T_{i=1,\ldots,n} \\
&= \left(\sum^n_{k=1}dq_k\sum^n_{j=1}\frac{\partial^2 F_i}{\partial q_j \partial q_k}\biggl|_\mathbf{q} {\dot q}_j \right)^T_{i=1,\ldots,n}
= \left(\sum^n_{j=1}\frac{\partial^2 F_i}{\partial q_j \partial q_k}\biggl|_\mathbf{q} {\dot q}_j \right)^n_{i,k=1}d\mathbf{q}.
\end{align}
</math>

In vector notation,
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
dL(\mathbf{Q},\dot\mathbf{Q},t)
&= \frac{\partial L}{\partial\mathbf{Q}}d\mathbf{Q}
+ \frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot\mathbf{Q}}d\dot\mathbf{Q}
+ \frac{\partial L}{\partial t}dt \\
&=\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial\mathbf{Q}}F_*(\mathbf{q}) + \frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot \mathbf{Q}}G(\mathbf{q},\dot\mathbf{q})\right)d\mathbf{q} + \frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot \mathbf{Q}} F_*(\mathbf{q})d\dot\mathbf{q} + \frac{\partial L}{\partial t}.
\end{align}
</math>

On the other hand,
<math display="block">
dL(\mathbf{q},\dot\mathbf{q},t)
= \frac{\partial L}{\partial\mathbf{q}}d\mathbf{q}
+ \frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot\mathbf{q}}d\dot\mathbf{q}
+ \frac{\partial L}{\partial t}dt.
</math>

It was mentioned earlier that Lagrangians do not depend on the choice of configuration space coordinates, i.e. <math>L(\mathbf{Q}, \dot\mathbf{Q}, t) = L(\mathbf{q},\dot\mathbf{q},t).</math> One implication of this is that <math>dL(\mathbf{Q}, \dot\mathbf{Q}, t) = dL(\mathbf{q},\dot\mathbf{q},t),</math> and
<math display="block">\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot\mathbf{Q}}F_*(\mathbf{q}) = \frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot\mathbf{q}}.</math>
This demonstrates that, for each <math>\mathbf{q},</math> <math>\dot\mathbf{q},</math> and <math>t,</math> <math>\textstyle \sum\limits^n_{i=1}\frac{\partial L}{\partial{\dot q}_i}d{\dot q}_i</math> is a well-defined linear form whose coefficients <math>\textstyle \frac{\partial L}{\partial{\dot q}_i}</math> are contravariant 1-tensors. Applying both sides of the equation to <math>\dot\mathbf{q}</math> and using the above formula for <math>\dot\mathbf{Q}</math> yields
<math display="block">\dot \mathbf{Q} \frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot\mathbf{Q}} = \dot \mathbf{q}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot\mathbf{q}}.</math>
The invariance of the energy <math>E</math> follows.
}}

==== Conservation ====
In Lagrangian mechanics, the system is [[closed system|closed]] if and only if its Lagrangian <math>L</math> does not explicitly depend on time. The [[energy conservation law]] states that the energy <math>E</math> of a closed system is an [[integral of motion]].

More precisely, let {{nowrap|1='''q''' = '''q'''(''t'')}} be an ''extremal''. (In other words, {{nowrap|'''q'''}} satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equations). Taking the total time-derivative of ''L'' along this extremal and using the EL equations leads to
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\frac{dL}{dt} &= \dot{\mathbf q} \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf q}+\ddot{\mathbf q} \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf \dot q} + \frac{\partial L}{\partial t} \\
- \frac{\partial L}{\partial t} &= \frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf \dot q}\right)\dot{\mathbf q}+\ddot{\mathbf q} \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf \dot q} - \dot{L} \\
- \frac{\partial L}{\partial t} &= \frac{d}{dt}\left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf \dot q} \mathbf \dot q  - L \right)= \frac{dH}{dt}
\end{align}</math>

If the Lagrangian ''L'' does not explicitly depend on time, then {{nowrap|1=∂''L''/∂''t'' = 0}}, then ''H'' does not vary with time evolution of particle, indeed, an integral of motion, meaning that
<math display="block">H(\mathbf{q}(t), \dot\mathbf{q}(t), t) = \text{constant of time}.</math>
Hence, if the chosen coordinates were natural coordinates, the energy is conserved.

==== Kinetic and potential energies ====
Under all these circumstances,<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Lifshitz|1976|page=14}}</ref> the constant
<math display="block">E = T + V </math>
is the total energy of the system. The kinetic and potential energies still change as the system evolves, but the motion of the system will be such that their sum, the total energy, is constant. This is a valuable simplification, since the energy ''E'' is a constant of integration that counts as an arbitrary constant for the problem, and it may be possible to integrate the velocities from this energy relation to solve for the coordinates.

=== Mechanical similarity ===
{{Main|Mechanical similarity}}

If the potential energy is a [[homogeneous function]] of the coordinates and independent of time,<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Lifshitz|1976|page=22}}</ref> and all position vectors are scaled by the same nonzero constant ''α'', {{nowrap|1='''r'''<sub>''k''</sub>&prime; = ''α'''''r'''<sub>''k''</sub>}}, so that
<math display="block">V(\alpha\mathbf{r}_1,\alpha\mathbf{r}_2,\ldots, \alpha\mathbf{r}_N)=\alpha^N V(\mathbf{r}_1,\mathbf{r}_2,\ldots, \mathbf{r}_N)</math>
and time is scaled by a factor ''β'', ''t''&prime; = ''βt'', then the velocities '''v'''<sub>''k''</sub> are scaled by a factor of ''α''/''β'' and the kinetic energy ''T'' by (''α''/''β'')<sup>2</sup>. The entire Lagrangian has been scaled by the same factor if
<math display="block">\frac{\alpha^2}{\beta^2}=\alpha^N \quad\Rightarrow\quad \beta = \alpha^{1-\frac{N}{2}}.</math>

Since the lengths and times have been scaled, the trajectories of the particles in the system follow geometrically similar paths differing in size. The length ''l'' traversed in time ''t'' in the original trajectory corresponds to a new length ''l''&prime; traversed in time ''t''&prime; in the new trajectory, given by the ratios
<math display="block">\frac{t'}{t}= \left(\frac{l'}{l}\right)^{1-\frac{N}{2}}.</math>

=== Interacting particles ===

For a given system, if two subsystems ''A'' and ''B'' are non-interacting, the Lagrangian ''L'' of the overall system is the sum of the Lagrangians ''L''<sub>''A''</sub> and ''L''<sub>''B''</sub> for the subsystems:<ref name="Landau 1976 page=4"/>
<math display="block">L = L_A + L_B. </math>

If they do interact this is not possible. In some situations, it may be possible to separate the Lagrangian of the system ''L'' into the sum of non-interacting Lagrangians, plus another Lagrangian ''L''<sub>''AB''</sub> containing information about the interaction,
<math display="block">L = L_A + L_B + L_{AB}.</math>

This may be physically motivated by taking the non-interacting Lagrangians to be kinetic energies only, while the interaction Lagrangian is the system's total potential energy. Also, in the limiting case of negligible interaction, ''L''<sub>''AB''</sub> tends to zero reducing to the non-interacting case above.

The extension to more than two non-interacting subsystems is straightforward – the overall Lagrangian is the sum of the separate Lagrangians for each subsystem. If there are interactions, then interaction Lagrangians may be added.

=== Strict convexity of Lagrangian ===
Since an infinitesimal variation of path <math>\delta q </math> can be made with arbitrary time parametrization, arbitrarily high variations in velocities can be achieved causing second order variation in action to be dominated by <math display="inline">\mathcal O(\delta \dot q)\gg \mathcal O(\delta q) </math> imposing the following condition by action minimization principle:<math display="block">\delta^2 S\geq 0\implies\frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial \dot q_i\partial \dot q_j}\delta \dot q_i\delta \dot q_j=(\delta q)^TW\delta q\geq 0 </math>which is the [[Positive semi-definite matrix|positive (semi) definiteness]] of the [[Hessian matrix]], <math display="inline">W_{ij}=\frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial \dot q_i\partial \dot q_j} </math> which is equivalent to the Lagrangian, <math>L </math>, being a [[convex function]] of generalized velocities.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-05-15|title=Lagrangians must be convex – Sufficiently wise|url=https://sufficientlywise.org/2017/05/15/lagrangians-must-be-convex/|access-date=2026-08-12|language=en-US}}</ref> Convexity of Lagrangian is of significance as it is also invariant under point transformations or modification of Lagrangian by total derivative terms.
{| class="toccolours collapsible collapsed" width="80%"
!Proof
|-
|If Lagrangian is modified by a total derivative <math display="inline">L'=L+\frac{d\lambda}{dt}=L+\frac{\partial \lambda}{\partial q}\dot q+\frac{\partial \lambda}{\partial t}</math>, the two Lagrangians share same Hessian and hence also preserve the convexity criteria.

Under point transformations, that are of the form <math display="inline">(q,\dot q,t)\rightarrow \left(Q(q,t),\dot Q(q,\dot q,t)=\frac{\partial Q}{\partial q}\dot q+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial t},t\right)</math>,<math display="block">q\rightarrow Q, \quad  \frac{\partial }{\partial \dot Q_r}=\frac{\partial \dot q_s}{\partial \dot Q_r}\frac{\partial }{\partial \dot q_s}=\frac{\partial q_s}{\partial Q_r}\frac{\partial }{\partial \dot q_s}\implies \frac{\partial^2 }{\partial \dot Q_r\partial \dot Q_s}=\frac{\partial q_\alpha}{\partial Q_r}\frac{\partial q_\beta}{\partial Q_s}\frac{\partial^2 }{\partial \dot q_\alpha\partial \dot q_\beta}</math>which ensures that convexity condition is invariant under point transformations. It additionally preserves systems having <math>\det(W)=0</math> condition, which are systems of physical relevance known as singular Lagrangians.
|}
A strictly convex Lagrangian require the condition to be always greater than zero, i.e. have an invertible Hessian matrix which are called non-singular Lagrangian systems. Strict convexity also enables passage from Lagrangian formulation to a Hamiltonian formulation that uses [[Poisson bracket]] structure through a [[Legendre transformation]], <math display="inline">L(q,\dot q,t)\rightarrow H(q,p=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q},t)</math> which is well defined on strictly convex functions. Lagrangian systems in Newtonian and special relativistic framework, with assumption of positive semi-definite Hessian of potential function, always have a strictly convex Lagrangian.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Williams|first=Anthony G.|date=2022-08-04|title=Introduction to Quantum Field Theory: Classical Mechanics to Gauge Field Theories|url=https://www.cambridge.org/highereducation/books/introduction-to-quantum-field-theory/6CF3EFCEC7B679B2519C40B2C2C962D8|access-date=2025-06-19|website=Higher Education from Cambridge University Press|language=en|doi=10.1017/9781108585286}}</ref>
{| class="toccolours collapsible collapsed" width="80%"
!Proof
|-
|Assumption

* The potential function has a hessian, <math>K_{rs} =- \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial \dot q^r\partial \dot q^s} </math>, with respect to generalized velocities that is either vanishing everywhere or positive (semi) definite everywhere. Note that this also applies to potentials that are linear in <math>\dot {\mathbf r}</math> such as that of electromagnetic field <math>V= \sum q(\phi - \dot {\mathbf r}\cdot \mathbf A)</math> since their hessian with respect to generalized velocities always vanish at every point.


Proof 1: Newtonian Mechanics

This follows from the expansion of the velocity vector in terms of generalized velocities, <math>\dot {\mathbf r}=\left (\frac {\partial \mathbf r}{\partial q^r}\dot q^r+\frac {\partial \mathbf r}{\partial t}\right)  </math>.

Assuming the form of the Lagrangian to be <math>L=T-V= \sum  \frac 1 2 m \dot {\mathbf r}^2-V </math> and substituting the expression for velocity vector, the hessian can be calculated to be: <math display="block">W_{rs} =\frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial \dot q^r\partial \dot q^s}=\sum m \frac{\partial \mathbf r}{\partial q^r}\cdot  \frac{\partial \mathbf r}{\partial q^s}+ K_{rs}=M_{rs}+K_{rs}</math>To show positive definiteness of the matrix, it is sufficient to show that <math>x^TMx=\sum m\left(\frac{\partial \mathbf r}{\partial q^s}x^s\right)^2> 0 </math> for any non zero <math>x^s</math> which is enforced by the bijective nature of generalized coordinates representing the configuration. This can be shown explicitly by enforcing that for any change in the values of coordinates, <math> q^s \rightarrow q^s + \epsilon x^s</math>, the corresponding change <math>\delta \mathbf r = \epsilon \frac{\partial \mathbf r}{\partial q^s}x^s</math> cannot be null vector for well-behaving generalized coordinates that are one-one representations which imposes non-zero magnitude square unless, <math>x = 0</math>. This property of generalized coordinates is called local invertibility in terms of physical configuration.

Hence it is also proved that <math>W</math> is a positive definite matrix implying strict convexity of Lagrangian of the given form in generalized velocity.

Proof 2: Special Relativity

Taking the relativistic Lagrangian, <math>L=- \sum \frac{m_0c^2}{\gamma(\dot{\mathbf r})}-V </math> and employing the same steps, the hessian of the Lagrangian is calculated to be: <math display="block"> W_{rs}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q^r \partial \dot q^s}=\sum {{\gamma (\dot{\mathbf r})}}\frac{\partial^2\left( \frac {m_0v^2}2\right)}{\partial \dot q^r \partial\dot q^s} +\sum \frac{m_0}{c^2} \gamma^3(\dot{\mathbf r})\frac{\partial\left( \frac {v^2}2\right)}{\partial\dot q^s} \frac{\partial \left( \frac {v^2}2\right)}{\partial \dot q^r }+K_{rs}=M'_{rs}+M_{rs}+K_{rs}</math> Since the first term is known to be positive definite, it is sufficient to show semi-positive definiteness of the second term which follows from:<math display="block">x^TMx=\sum \frac{m_0}{c^2}\gamma^3(\dot{\mathbf r})\left(\frac{\partial \left( \frac {v^2}2\right)}{\partial \dot q^s } x^s \right)^2 \geq 0  </math>Hence it is proved that <math>W</math> is positive definite matrix implying strict convexity of Lagrangian of the given form in generalized velocity.<ref name=":1" />

In general relativity however, <math>L=\sqrt{g_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu \dot x^\nu}\implies \partial_{\dot x^\mu}\partial_{\dot x^\nu}L=(g_{\mu\nu}\dot x\cdot\dot x-g_{\mu\alpha}g_{\nu\beta}\dot x^{\alpha}\dot x^\beta)L^{-3} </math> which has null eigenvector <math>\dot x^\nu </math>.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Are the Hamiltonian and Lagrangian always convex functions?|url=https://physics.stackexchange.com/questions/103997/are-the-hamiltonian-and-lagrangian-always-convex-functions/339516#339516|access-date=2026-08-12|website=Physics Stack Exchange|language=en}}</ref>
|}

=== Singular Lagrangians ===
{{See also|Dirac bracket}}
Due to invariance of the non-singularity of the Hessian matrix, <math display="inline">W_{ij}=\frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial \dot q_i\partial \dot q_j} </math>, over coordinate transformations and modification of Lagrangian by total derivatives, such cases are physically relevant and are called singular Lagrangians. Since [[Canonical transformation|canonical transformations]] in Hamiltonian dynamics are a greater set of transformations than the corresponding point transformations, singularity of Hamiltonians is not generally invariant under it.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |date=1982|title=Constrained Dynamics|url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/BFb0036225|journal=Lecture Notes in Physics|language=en|doi=10.1007/bfb0036225}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Carcassi|first=Gabriele|url=https://www.fulcrum.org/concern/monographs/tx31qm110|title=Assumptions of Physics|last2=Aidala|first2=Christine A.|date=2021|publisher=Maize Books|isbn=978-1-60785-703-7|language=en|doi=10.3998/mpub.12204707}}</ref> The Jacobian of the transformation, <math display="inline">(q,\dot q, t)\rightarrow (q,p,t)</math>, is also the singular Hessian matrix, <math display="inline">W_{ij}</math>. Thus, the non-invertibility of transformation to phase space is expressed as only a sub-manifold of the phase space that is characterized by constraint equations, corresponding to physical states and their corresponding dynamics, due to which it is also sometimes termed as constrained dynamics.<ref name=":2" />

From the Euler-Lagrange equations, it follows that:<math display="block">\begin{align}
&\frac{d}{d t}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot{q}_{i}}-\frac{\partial L} {\partial q_{i}}=0\implies\sum_{j}W_{i j}(q,\dot{q},t)\ddot{q}_{j}={\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_{i}}}-\frac{\partial L}{\partial t}-\sum_{j}{\frac{\partial^{2}L}{\partial\dot{q}_{i}\partial q_{j}}}\dot{q}_{j},\\
\end{align}</math>where non-singularity of the Hessian, <math display="inline">W</math>, allows the above equations to solve all generalized accelerations as functions of <math>(q,\dot q, t)</math>.<ref name=":2" /> Hence, non-singularity of the Lagrangian is to be expected when not all <math>\ddot q</math> can be solved in terms of <math>(q,\dot q, t)</math> or if first order derivatives are the highest order derivative in some combinations of the equations of motions. For example, these are encountered in classical field theory Lagrangians of [[Schrödinger equation|Schrodinger's equation]] and [[Dirac equation]] whose equation of motion are first order in time derivative, and of [[Electromagnetism|classical electromagnetic theory]] since <math>\partial_t^2 A^0</math> is absent in [[Maxwell's equations]].<ref name=":2" />

Under certain assumptions, it is possible to obtain a consistent Hamiltonian formulation, but with a modified form of the transformation generating Lie brackets, such as [[Dirac bracket]] for theories whose rank of the Hessian matrix remains constant.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Mukunda|first=N|date=1976-08-01|title=Symmetries and constraints in generalized Hamiltonian dynamics|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0003491676901019|journal=Annals of Physics|volume=99|issue=2|pages=408–433|doi=10.1016/0003-4916(76)90101-9|issn=0003-4916|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Thus [[canonical quantization]] makes use of preservation of the corresponding Lie algebra structure (upto an overall central charge) to derive an appropriate quantum representations which, for constrained systems results in canonical relations that differ from that expected from Poisson brackets.<ref name=":1" />

== Examples ==

The following examples apply Lagrange's equations of the second kind to mechanical problems.

=== Conservative force ===

A particle of mass ''m'' moves under the influence of a [[conservative force]] derived from the [[gradient]] ∇ of a [[scalar potential]],
<math display="block">\mathbf{F} = -\boldsymbol{\nabla} V(\mathbf{r}).</math>

If there are more particles, in accordance with the above results, the total kinetic energy is a sum over all the particle kinetic energies, and the potential is a function of all the coordinates.

==== Cartesian coordinates ====

The Lagrangian of the particle can be written
<math display="block">L(x,y,z, \dot{x}, \dot{y},\dot{z}) = \frac{1}{2} m (\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2 + \dot{z}^2) - V(x,y,z).</math>

The equations of motion for the particle are found by applying the [[Euler–Lagrange equation]], for the ''x'' coordinate
<math display="block">\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} \left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{x}} \right) = \frac{\partial L}{\partial x}, </math>
with derivatives
<math display="block">\frac{\partial L}{\partial x} = - \frac{\partial V}{\partial x},\quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{x}}  = m \dot{x},\quad \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} \left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{x}} \right) = m \ddot{x},</math>
hence
<math display="block">m \ddot{x} = - \frac{\partial V}{\partial x},</math>
and similarly for the ''y'' and ''z'' coordinates. Collecting the equations in vector form we find
<math display="block">m\ddot{\mathbf{r}}=-\boldsymbol{\nabla} V</math>
which is [[Newton's second law of motion]] for a particle subject to a conservative force.

==== Polar coordinates in 2D and 3D ====

Using the spherical coordinates {{nowrap|(''r'', ''θ'', ''φ'')}} as commonly used in physics (ISO&nbsp;80000-2:2019 convention), where ''r'' is the radial distance to origin, ''θ'' is polar angle  (also known as colatitude, zenith angle, normal angle, or inclination angle), and ''φ'' is the azimuthal angle, the Lagrangian for a central potential is
<math display="block">L = \frac{m}{2}(\dot{r}^2+r^2\dot{\theta}^2 +r^2\sin^2\theta \, \dot{\varphi}^2)-V(r).</math>
So, in spherical coordinates, the Euler–Lagrange equations are
<math display="block">m\ddot{r}-mr(\dot{\theta}^2+\sin^2\theta \, \dot{\varphi}^2)+\frac{\partial V}{\partial r} =0,</math>
<math display="block">\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(mr^2\dot{\theta}) -mr^2\sin\theta\cos\theta \, \dot{\varphi}^2=0,</math>
<math display="block">\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(mr^2\sin^2\theta \, \dot{\varphi})=0.</math>
The ''φ'' coordinate is cyclic since it does not appear in the Lagrangian, so the conserved momentum in the system is the angular momentum
<math display="block">p_\varphi = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\varphi}} = mr^2\sin^2\theta \dot{\varphi},</math>
in which ''r'', ''θ'' and ''dφ''/''dt'' can all vary with time, but only in such a way that ''p''<sub>''φ''</sub> is constant.

The Lagrangian in two-dimensional polar coordinates is recovered by fixing ''θ'' to the constant value ''π''/2.

=== Pendulum on a movable support ===
[[File:pendulumWithMovableSupport.svg|thumb|right|250px|Sketch of the situation with definition of the coordinates (click to enlarge)]]

Consider a pendulum of mass ''m'' and length ''ℓ'', which is attached to a support with mass ''M'', which can move along a line in the <math>x</math>-direction. Let <math>x</math> be the coordinate along the line of the support, and let us denote the position of the pendulum by the angle <math>\theta</math> from the vertical. The coordinates and velocity components of the pendulum bob are
<math display="block">\begin{array}{rll}
& x_\mathrm{pend} = x + \ell \sin \theta & \quad \Rightarrow \quad \dot{x}_\mathrm{pend} = \dot{x} + \ell \dot{\theta} \cos \theta \\
& y_\mathrm{pend} = - \ell \cos\theta & \quad \Rightarrow \quad \dot{y}_\mathrm{pend} = \ell \dot{\theta} \sin \theta.
\end{array}</math>

The generalized coordinates can be taken to be <math>x</math> and <math>\theta</math>. The kinetic energy of the system is then
<math display="block">T = \frac{1}{2} M \dot{x}^2 + \frac{1}{2} m \left( \dot{x}_\mathrm{pend}^2 + \dot{y}_\mathrm{pend}^2 \right)</math>
and the potential energy is
<math display="block"> V = m g y_\mathrm{pend}  </math>
giving the Lagrangian
<math display="block">\begin{array}{rcl}
L &=& T - V \\
&=& \frac{1}{2} M \dot{x}^2 + \frac{1}{2} m \left[ \left( \dot x + \ell \dot\theta \cos \theta \right)^2 + \left( \ell \dot\theta \sin \theta \right)^2 \right] + m g \ell \cos \theta \\
&=& \frac{1}{2} \left(  M + m \right) \dot x^2 + m \dot x \ell \dot \theta \cos \theta + \frac{1}{2} m \ell^2 \dot \theta ^2 + m g \ell \cos \theta.
\end{array}</math>

Since ''x'' is absent from the Lagrangian, it is a cyclic coordinate. The conserved momentum is
<math display="block">p_x = \frac{\partial L }{\partial \dot{x}} = (M + m) \dot x + m \ell \dot\theta \cos\theta,</math>
and the Lagrange equation for the support coordinate <math>x</math> is
<math display="block">  (M + m) \ddot x + m \ell \ddot\theta\cos\theta-m \ell \dot\theta ^2 \sin\theta = 0.</math>

The Lagrange equation for the angle ''θ'' is
<math display="block">\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left[ m( \dot x \ell \cos\theta + \ell^2 \dot\theta ) \right] + m \ell (\dot x \dot \theta + g) \sin\theta = 0;</math>
and simplifying
<math display="block">\ddot\theta + \frac{\ddot x}{\ell} \cos\theta + \frac{g}{\ell} \sin\theta = 0.</math>

These equations may look quite complicated, but finding them with Newton's laws would have required carefully identifying all forces, which would have been much more laborious and prone to errors.
