By considering limit cases, the correctness of this system can be verified: For example, <math>\ddot x \to 0</math> should give the equations of motion for a [[simple pendulum]] that is at rest in some [[inertial frame]], while <math>\ddot\theta \to 0</math> should give the equations for a pendulum in a constantly accelerating system, etc. Furthermore, it is trivial to obtain the results numerically, given suitable starting conditions and a chosen time step, by [[Numerical ordinary differential equations|stepping through the results iteratively]].

=== Two-body central force problem ===
{{main|Two-body problem|Central force}}

Two bodies of masses {{math|''m''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{math|''m''<sub>2</sub>}} with position vectors {{math|'''r'''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{math|'''r'''<sub>2</sub>}} are in orbit about each other due to an attractive [[central potential]] {{math|''V''}}. We may write down the Lagrangian in terms of the position coordinates as they are, but it is an established procedure to convert the two-body problem into a one-body problem as follows. Introduce the [[Jacobi coordinates]]; the separation of the bodies {{math|1='''r''' = '''r'''<sub>2</sub> − '''r'''<sub>1</sub>}} and the location of the [[center of mass]] {{math|1='''R''' = (''m''<sub>1</sub>'''r'''<sub>1</sub> + ''m''<sub>2</sub>'''r'''<sub>2</sub>)/(''m''<sub>1</sub> + ''m''<sub>2</sub>)}}. The Lagrangian is then<ref>{{harvnb|Taylor|2005|page=297}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Padmanabhan|2000|edition=3rd|page=48 }}</ref><ref group = nb>The Lagrangian also can be written explicitly for a rotating frame. See Padmanabhan, 2000.</ref>
<math display="block">
L = \underbrace{\frac {1}{2} M \dot{\mathbf{R}}^2}_{L_{\text{cm}}} + \underbrace{\frac {1}{2} \mu \dot{\mathbf{r}}^2 - V(|\mathbf{r}|) }_{L_{\text{rel}}}</math>
where {{math|1=''M'' = ''m''<sub>1</sub> + ''m''<sub>2</sub>}} is the total mass, {{math|1=''μ'' = ''m''<sub>1</sub>''m''<sub>2</sub>/(''m''<sub>1</sub> + ''m''<sub>2</sub>)}} is the [[reduced mass]], and {{math|''V''}} the potential of the radial force, which depends only on the [[Norm (mathematics)|magnitude]] of the separation {{math|1={{abs|'''r'''}} = {{abs|'''r'''<sub>2</sub> − '''r'''<sub>1</sub>}}}}. The Lagrangian splits into a ''center-of-mass'' term {{math|''L''<sub>cm</sub>}} and a ''relative motion'' term {{math|''L''<sub>rel</sub>}}.

The Euler–Lagrange equation for {{math|'''R'''}} is simply
<math display="block">M\ddot{\mathbf{R}} = 0, </math>
which states the center of mass moves in a straight line at constant velocity.

Since the relative motion only depends on the magnitude of the separation, it is ideal to use polar coordinates {{math|(''r'', ''θ'')}} and take {{math|1=''r'' = {{abs|'''r'''}}}},
<math display="block">L_\text{rel} = \frac{1}{2} \mu \left(\dot{r}^2 +r^2 \dot{\theta}^2 \right) - V(r), </math>
so {{math|''θ''}} is a cyclic coordinate with the corresponding conserved (angular) momentum
<math display="block">p_\theta = \frac {\partial L_\text{rel}}{\partial \dot \theta} = \mu r^2 \dot \theta = \ell. </math>

The radial coordinate {{math|''r''}} and angular velocity {{math|d''θ''/d''t''}} can vary with time, but only in such a way that {{math|''ℓ''}} is constant. The Lagrange equation for {{math|''r''}} is
<math display="block">\mu r \dot \theta ^2 -\frac {dV}{dr} = \mu \ddot{r}. </math>

This equation is identical to the radial equation obtained using Newton's laws in a ''co-rotating'' reference frame, that is, a frame rotating with the reduced mass so it appears stationary. Eliminating the angular velocity {{math|d''θ''/d''t''}} from this radial equation,<ref>{{harvnb|Hand|Finch|1998|pages=140–141}}</ref>
<math display="block">\mu \ddot r = -\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}r} + \frac{\ell^2}{\mu r^3}. </math>
which is the equation of motion for a one-dimensional problem in which a particle of mass {{math|''μ''}} is subjected to the inward central force {{math|−d''V''/d''r''}} and a second outward force, called in this context the ''(Lagrangian) centrifugal force'' (see [[centrifugal force#Other uses of the term]]):
<math display="block">F_{\mathrm{cf}} = \mu r \dot \theta ^2 = \frac {\ell^2}{\mu r^3}. </math>

Of course, if one remains entirely within the one-dimensional formulation, {{math|''ℓ''}} enters only as some imposed parameter of the external outward force, and its interpretation as angular momentum depends upon the more general two-dimensional problem from which the one-dimensional problem originated.

If one arrives at this equation using Newtonian mechanics in a co-rotating frame, the interpretation is evident as the centrifugal force in that frame due to the rotation of the frame itself. If one arrives at this equation directly by using the generalized coordinates {{math|(''r'', ''θ'')}} and simply following the Lagrangian formulation without thinking about frames at all, the interpretation is that the centrifugal force is an outgrowth of ''using polar coordinates''. As Hildebrand says:<ref>{{harvnb|Hildebrand|1992 |page=156}}</ref>

"Since such quantities are not true physical forces, they are often called ''inertia forces''. Their presence or absence depends, not upon the particular problem at hand, but ''upon the coordinate system chosen''." In particular, if Cartesian coordinates are chosen, the centrifugal force disappears, and the formulation involves only the central force itself, which provides the [[centripetal force]] for a curved motion.

This viewpoint, that fictitious forces originate in the choice of coordinates, often is expressed by users of the Lagrangian method. This view arises naturally in the Lagrangian approach, because the frame of reference is (possibly unconsciously) selected by the choice of coordinates. For example, see<ref>{{harvnb|Zak|Zbilut|Meyers|1997|pages=202}}</ref> for a comparison of Lagrangians in an inertial and in a noninertial frame of reference. See also the discussion of "total" and "updated" Lagrangian formulations in.<ref>{{harvnb|Shabana|2008|pages=118–119}}</ref> Unfortunately, this usage of "inertial force" conflicts with the Newtonian idea of an inertial force. In the Newtonian view, an inertial force originates in the acceleration of the frame of observation (the fact that it is not an [[inertial frame of reference]]), not in the choice of coordinate system. To keep matters clear, it is safest to refer to the Lagrangian inertial forces as ''generalized'' inertial forces, to distinguish them from the Newtonian vector inertial forces. That is, one should avoid following Hildebrand when he says (p.&nbsp;155) "we deal ''always'' with ''generalized'' forces, velocities accelerations, and momenta. For brevity, the adjective "generalized" will be omitted frequently."

It is known that the Lagrangian of a system is not unique. Within the Lagrangian formalism the Newtonian fictitious forces can be identified by the existence of alternative Lagrangians in which the fictitious forces disappear, sometimes found by exploiting the symmetry of the system.<ref>{{harvnb|Gannon|2006 |page=267}}</ref>

== Extensions to include non-conservative forces ==

=== Dissipative forces ===
[[Dissipation]] (i.e. non-conservative systems) can also be treated with an effective Lagrangian formulated by a certain doubling of the degrees of freedom.<ref>{{harvnb|Kosyakov|2007}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Galley|2013}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Birnholtz|Hadar|Kol|2014}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Birnholtz|Hadar|Kol|2013}}</ref>

In a more general formulation, the forces could be both conservative and [[viscosity|viscous]]. If an appropriate transformation can be found from the '''F'''<sub>''i''</sub>, [[John Strutt, 3rd Baron Rayleigh|Rayleigh]] suggests using a [[Rayleigh dissipation function|dissipation function]], ''D'', of the following form:<ref name="Torby 1984 page=271">{{harvnb|Torby|1984|page=271}}</ref>
<math display="block">D = \frac {1}{2} \sum_{j=1}^m \sum_{k=1}^m C_{j k} \dot{q}_j \dot{q}_k,</math>
where ''C''<sub>''jk''</sub> are constants that are related to the damping coefficients in the physical system, though not necessarily equal to them. If ''D'' is defined this way, then<ref name="Torby 1984 page=271"/>
<math display="block">Q_j = - \frac {\partial V}{\partial q_j} - \frac {\partial D}{\partial \dot{q}_j}</math>
and
<math display="block"> \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} \left ( \frac {\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_j} \right ) - \frac {\partial L}{\partial q_j} + \frac {\partial D}{\partial \dot{q}_j} = 0.</math>

=== Electromagnetism ===
A test particle is a particle whose [[mass]] and [[electric charge|charge]] are assumed to be so small that its effect on external system is insignificant. It is often a hypothetical simplified point particle with no properties other than mass and charge. Real particles like [[electron]]s and [[up quark]]s are more complex and have additional terms in their Lagrangians. Not only can the fields form non conservative potentials, these potentials can also be velocity dependent.

The Lagrangian for a [[charged particle]] with [[electrical charge]] {{math|''q''}}, interacting with an [[electromagnetic field]], is the prototypical example of a velocity-dependent potential. The electric [[scalar potential]] {{math|''ϕ'' {{=}} ''ϕ''('''r''', ''t'')}} and [[magnetic vector potential]] {{math|1='''A''' = '''A'''('''r''', ''t'')}} are defined from the [[electric field]] {{math|1='''E''' = '''E'''('''r''', ''t'')}} and [[magnetic field]] {{math|1='''B''' = '''B'''('''r''', ''t'')}} as follows:
<math display="block">\mathbf{E} = - \boldsymbol{\nabla}\phi - \frac{\partial \mathbf{A}}{\partial t}, \quad \mathbf{B} = \boldsymbol{\nabla} \times \mathbf{A}. </math>

The Lagrangian of a massive charged test particle in an electromagnetic field
<math display="block"> L = \tfrac{1}{2}m \dot{\mathbf{r}}^2 + q\, \dot{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \mathbf{A} - q \phi,</math>
is called [[minimal coupling]]. This is a good example of when the common [[rule of thumb]] that the Lagrangian is the kinetic energy minus the potential energy is incorrect. Combined with [[Euler–Lagrange equation]], it produces the [[Lorentz force]] law
<math display="block">m \ddot{\mathbf{r}} = q \mathbf{E} + q \dot{\mathbf{r}} \times \mathbf{B} </math>

Under [[gauge transformation]]:
<math display="block">\mathbf{A} \rightarrow \mathbf{A}+\boldsymbol{\nabla} f, \quad \phi \rightarrow \phi-\dot f, </math>
where {{math|''f''('''r''',''t'')}} is any scalar function of space and time, the aforementioned Lagrangian transforms like:
<math display="block">L \rightarrow L+q\left(\dot{\mathbf{r}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\nabla}+\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\right)f=L+q\frac{df}{dt}, </math>
which still produces the same Lorentz force law.

Note that the [[canonical momentum]] (conjugate to position {{math|'''r'''}}) is the [[kinetic momentum]] plus a contribution from the {{math|'''A'''}} field (known as the potential momentum):
<math display="block">\mathbf{p} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\mathbf{r}}} = m \dot{\mathbf{r}} + q \mathbf{A}. </math>

This relation is also used in the [[minimal coupling]] prescription in [[quantum mechanics]] and [[quantum field theory]]. From this expression, we can see that the [[canonical momentum]] {{math|'''p'''}} is not gauge invariant, and therefore not a measurable physical quantity; However, if {{math|'''r'''}} is cyclic (i.e. Lagrangian is independent of position {{math|'''r'''}}), which happens if the {{math|''ϕ''}} and {{math|'''A'''}} fields are uniform, then this canonical momentum {{math|'''p'''}} given here is the conserved momentum, while the measurable physical kinetic momentum {{math|''m'''''v'''}} is not.

== Other contexts and formulations ==

The ideas in Lagrangian mechanics have numerous applications in other areas of physics, and can adopt generalized results from the calculus of variations.

=== Alternative formulations of classical mechanics ===

A closely related formulation of classical mechanics is [[Hamiltonian mechanics]]. The Hamiltonian is defined by
<math display="block"> H = \sum_{i=1}^n \dot{q}_i\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_i} - L</math>
and can be obtained by performing a [[Legendre transformation]] on the Lagrangian, which introduces new variables [[Canonical coordinates|canonically conjugate]] to the original variables. For example, given a set of generalized coordinates, the variables [[canonical coordinates|canonically conjugate]] are the generalized momenta. This doubles the number of variables, but makes differential equations first order. The Hamiltonian is a particularly ubiquitous quantity in [[quantum mechanics]] (see [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)]]).

[[Routhian mechanics]] is a hybrid formulation of Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics, which is not often used in practice but an efficient formulation for cyclic coordinates.

=== Momentum space formulation ===
{{main|Position and momentum space#Lagrangian mechanics}}

The Euler–Lagrange equations can also be formulated in terms of the generalized momenta rather than generalized coordinates. Performing a Legendre transformation on the generalized coordinate Lagrangian {{nowrap|''L''('''q''', d'''q'''/d''t'', ''t'')}} obtains the generalized momenta Lagrangian {{nowrap|''L''&prime;('''p''', d'''p'''/d''t'', ''t'')}} in terms of the original Lagrangian, as well the EL equations in terms of the generalized momenta. Both Lagrangians contain the same information, and either can be used to solve for the motion of the system. In practice generalized coordinates are more convenient to use and interpret than generalized momenta.

=== Alternative Lagrangians ===

Since Lagrangians that differ by a total time derivative term <math display="inline"> \frac{d f(x,t)}{dt} </math> produce the same equations of motion,<ref>{{Citation |chapter=Lagrangian Formulation of Mechanics |date=1998 |title=Classical Dynamics: A Contemporary Approach |pages=48–107 |editor-last=Saletan |editor-first=Eugene J. |editor2-last=José |editor2-first=Jorge V. |place=Cambridge |publisher=Cambridge University Press |doi=10.1017/CBO9780511803772.003 |isbn=978-0-521-63636-0 }}</ref> it is possible to write the traditional one-dimensional Lagrangian, <math display="inline"> L = T-U, </math> in the equivalent form

<math display="block"> L_a = \left( \sqrt{T} \pm i \sqrt{U} \right)^2</math>

where it is assumed that, everywhere between the fixed endpoints, the kinetic energy is of the form <math display="inline"> T = a(x)\dot{x}^2 \geq 0 </math> and <math display="inline">U(x) \geq 0</math>. For a kinetic energy <math display="inline"> T = m\dot{x}^2/2 \geq 0 </math>, the resulting equation of motion is

<math display="block">\sqrt{\frac{m}{2}} \dot{x} \pm i\sqrt{U}  =  A \exp \left[ \pm i \sqrt{\frac{2}{m}}  \int \frac{\partial \sqrt{U}}{\partial x}dt\right]</math>

This equation provides a [[phasor]] picture of the energy of the system. The phasor has a magnitude equal to the square root of the total energy, and it rotates between the <math display="inline">\sqrt{\frac{m}{2}}\dot{x} </math> and <math display="inline">\sqrt{U}</math> axes at an angle <math display="inline">\sqrt{\frac{2}{m}}  \int \frac{\partial \sqrt{U}}{\partial x}dt</math>. Thus the transfer of energy from potential to kinetic is conveyed by rotations of the phasor.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zengel |first1=Keith |title=An Alternative Lagrangian Approach |journal=Am. J. Phys. |date=2026 |volume=94 |page=248-252 |doi=10.1119/5.0307168}}</ref>

=== Alternative Actions ===
It is possible to show, using [[Lagrange multiplier]] techniques<ref name="zengel1">{{cite journal |last1=Zengel |first1=Keith |title=Why the action? |journal=Am. J. Phys. |date=2024 |volume=92 |pages=885-888 |doi=10.1119/5.0199741}}</ref> and other techniques,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gray |first1=G.G. |last2=Karl |first2=G. |last3=Novikov |first3=V.A. |title=The Four Variational Principles of Mechanics |journal=Annals of Physics |date=1996 |volume=251 |page=1-25 |doi=10.1006/aphy.1996.0104}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gray |first1=C. G. |last2=Karl |first2=G. |last3=Novikov |first3=V. A. |title=KarlProgress in classical and quantum variational principles |journal=Rep. Prog. Phys. |date=2004 |volume=67 |page=159-208 |doi=10.1088/0034-4885/67/2/R02|arxiv=physics/0312071 }}</ref> that many alternative actions may be used to produce the same equations of motion as the traditional action. These alternative actions are typically formulated with the assumption that time averaged values of the total energy are fixed. It is also possible to assume that time-averaged values of the kinetic or potential energies are fixed. For example, consider the actions

<math display="block">S_T =\int  T  \,dt  + \lambda_T \left[ \int \left( T + U\right) \,dt  - \bar{E}\Delta t\right],</math>

and 

<math display="block">S_U = \int U \,dt  + \lambda_U \left[ \int \left( T + U\right) \,dt  - \bar{E}\Delta t\right]. </math>

The terms in the square brackets represent the constraint that the time-averaged value of <math display="inline">T+U</math> over the interval <math display="inline">\Delta t</math> must be <math display="inline">\bar{E}</math>. Both actions produce the same equations of motion as each other and as the traditional action for <math display="inline">\lambda_T = -1/2</math> and <math display="inline">\lambda_U = -1/2</math>, which are also the values for which the total energy <math display="inline">T+U</math> is at all times equal to the time-averaged energy <math display="inline">\bar{E}</math>. 

One interesting feature of <math display="inline">S_T</math> is that its extremal value is a minimum value in the typical case where <math display="inline">T = \frac{1}{2} m \dot{x}^2</math>. This is true since the square bracketed constraint term in the action is, by definition, constant, and the second variation of the action will have the form <math display="inline">\delta^2 S_T = \int m \dot{\eta}^2\, dt </math>, where <math display="inline">\eta</math> is the variation of the path. Clearly <math display="inline">\delta^2 S_T \geq 0</math> for any <math display="inline">\eta</math>, so the extremal value must be a minimum.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gelfand |first1=I. M. |last2=Fomin |first2=S. V. |title=Calculus of Variations |date=1963 |publisher=Prentice-Hall |location=Englewood Cliffs, N.J. |pages=42-43 and 100-101}}</ref>

Additionally, one might consider actions consisting of products of time-integrals of energy. For example and product action with a constraint on the time-averaged energy

<math display="block">S_P = \left[\int  T  \,dt \right]\left[\int  U  \,dt \right] + \lambda_P \left[ \int \left( T + U\right) \,dt  - \bar{E}\Delta t\right]</math>

will produce the same equations of motion as the traditional action, for the appropriate choice of <math display="inline">\lambda_P</math>. It is also possible to produce the traditional equations of motion for powers of products of time-integrated energies, such as

<math display="block">S_{nm} = \left[\int  T  \,dt \right]^n \left[\int  U  \,dt \right]^m + \lambda_{nm} \left[ \int \left( T + U\right) \,dt  - \bar{E}\Delta t\right]</math>

so long as the appropriate value of <math display="inline">\lambda_{nm}</math> is chosen.<ref name="zengel1">{{cite journal |last1=Zengel |first1=Keith |title=Why the action? |journal=Am. J. Phys. |date=2024 |volume=92 |pages=885-888 |doi=10.1119/5.0199741}}</ref>

=== Higher derivatives of generalized coordinates ===

There is no mathematical reason to restrict the derivatives of generalized coordinates to first order only. It is possible to derive modified EL equations for a Lagrangian containing higher order derivatives, see [[Euler–Lagrange equation]] for details. However, from the physical point-of-view there is an obstacle to include time derivatives higher than the first order, which is implied by Ostrogradsky's construction of a canonical formalism for nondegenerate higher derivative Lagrangians, see [[Ostrogradsky instability]]

=== Optics ===

{{main|Hamiltonian optics}}

Lagrangian mechanics can be applied to [[geometrical optics]], by applying variational principles to rays of light in a medium, and solving the EL equations gives the equations of the paths the light rays follow.

=== Relativistic formulation ===
{{main|Relativistic Lagrangian mechanics}}

Lagrangian mechanics can be formulated in [[special relativity]] and [[general relativity]]. Some features of Lagrangian mechanics are retained in the relativistic theories but difficulties quickly appear in other respects. In particular, the EL equations take the same form, and the connection between cyclic coordinates and conserved momenta still applies, however the Lagrangian must be modified and is not simply the kinetic minus the potential energy of a particle. Also, it is not straightforward to handle multiparticle systems in a [[manifestly covariant]] way, it may be possible if a particular frame of reference is singled out.

=== Quantum mechanics ===

In [[quantum mechanics]], [[action (physics)|action]] and quantum-mechanical [[phase (waves)|phase]] are related via the [[Planck constant]], and the [[principle of stationary action]] can be understood in terms of [[constructive interference]] of [[wave function]]s.

In 1948, [[Richard Feynman|Feynman]] discovered the [[path integral formulation]] extending the [[principle of least action]] to [[quantum mechanics]] for [[electrons]] and [[photons]]. In this formulation, particles travel every possible path between the initial and final states; the probability of a specific final state is obtained by summing over all possible trajectories leading to it. In the classical regime, the path integral formulation cleanly reproduces Hamilton's principle, and [[Fermat's principle]] in [[optics]].

=== Classical field theory ===

In Lagrangian mechanics, the generalized coordinates form a discrete set of variables that define the configuration of a system. In [[classical field theory]], the physical system is not a set of discrete particles, but rather a continuous field {{nowrap|''ϕ''('''r''', ''t'')}} defined over a region of 3D space. Associated with the field is a [[Lagrangian density]]
<math display="block">\mathcal{L}(\phi, \nabla \phi, \dot\phi, \mathbf{r},t)</math>
defined in terms of the field and its space and time derivatives at a location '''r''' and time ''t''. Analogous to the particle case, for non-relativistic applications the Lagrangian density is also the kinetic energy density of the field, minus its potential energy density (this is not true in general, and the Lagrangian density has to be "reverse engineered"). The Lagrangian is then the [[volume integral]] of the Lagrangian density over 3D space
<math display="block"> L(t) = \int  \mathcal{L} \, \mathrm{d}^3 \mathbf{r} </math>
where d<sup>3</sup>'''r''' is a 3D [[Total differential#Differentials in several variables|differential]] [[volume element]]. The Lagrangian is a function of time since the Lagrangian density has implicit space dependence via the fields, and may have explicit spatial dependence, but these are removed in the integral, leaving only time in as the variable for the Lagrangian.

=== Noether's theorem ===

The action principle, and the Lagrangian formalism, are tied closely to [[Noether's theorem]], which connects physical [[conserved quantity|conserved quantities]] to continuous [[symmetry (physics)|symmetries]] of a physical system.

If the Lagrangian is invariant under a symmetry, then the resulting equations of motion are also invariant under that symmetry. This characteristic is very helpful in showing that theories are consistent with either [[special relativity]] or [[general relativity]].
